(Appalachia 08)

docs.title: Continuity
docs.text:
• Continues straight from the crash site in Appalachia 07.
  • Kurt says the team has "already tested an ape-man" and knows it had a human father. No recorded episode shows that test, which places it in the unrecorded Appalachia 05.
  • The players recall the surveillance equipment in the Clinton story only as "surveillance equipment"; Dante points out that the night-vision goggles were seen in the cold open of Appalachia 06, not by the characters.
  • The Biz has no bug left to plant on Jan. Dante's joke is that he "used them all up on Clinton".
  • Jan says he grew up in East Germany. The investigator guessed "Polish or Irish or something", and the players call him "that goddamn Polish guy" regardless.
  • Andre says here that the sheriff "dived into the break room". In Appalachia 09 he adds that "it was never a break room. It was just a door": the room behind it held the caged ape-men, and the door itself was blown away by the Claymore.
  • Leads directly into Appalachia 09.

(Appalachia 08)

docs.title: The Things in Appalachia, Episode 09
docs.text:
Sealed in the Spud Hut basement, the team learns the whole scheme from an animal handler named Clive, drugs a shift of ape-man miners with ketamine-filled Combos, finds a crack in the air, kills Big Bob and climbs out into the woods, while Jan Martense drives away.

Arc The Things in Appalachia Episode 09 (the last recorded session of the arc) Setting Beneath the Spud Hut Georgia Regional Distribution Center and in the Dahlonega gold mines In-fiction date October 1992, continuing from the last moment of Appalachia 08 Players present Andre (GM), Dante, Ezra, Zack, Rita; Ben listening in Previous Appalachia 08 Next Appalachia 10 (unrecorded)

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: With the elevator locked off and Huell Kendrick badly hurt, the team frees Clive, a large-animal handler shut in the kennel office. He explains that Jan Martense has been using ape-men to mine the gold left under Dahlonega. The only way out is through the mines: past a room of gold bars, a crack in the air pumping gas into the tunnels, a working shift of ape-men, and a hunter called Big Bob. (Appalachia 09)

docs.title: Trapped
docs.text:
Sheriff Carter Burke is screaming in the middle of the group until Kurt Larson clamps his hands over his head and asks him politely to stop (Manipulate Someone, 11). Andrew Howard lies in gore, unhurt, holding a camera with a shattered lens. The elevator has not come back; its maintenance ladder is behind a grate and a steel shutter, and the power is out. A piece of ape-man jawbone, teeth and all, is pulled out of Huell's buttock. Kurt's Preparedness roll (12) produces cocaine, which he applies to the wound; Huell goes numb and is now high. (Appalachia 09)

Andrew's delight in the creatures makes the sheriff worse. He believes the agents are Men in Black who released the ape-men and spied on the presidential candidate. The Biz uses his Grifter move to learn what would convince him, and on an 8 wins the sheriff's conditional cooperation by sorting the room into "car guy", "poker guy" and "freak guy". (Appalachia 09)

docs.title: Clive and the operation
docs.text:
A voice calls from down the hall. Past veterinary gear, strapped gurneys, mining equipment and a kennel room, Kurt and Andrew find a man behind a locked wired-glass door, alarmed to hear that "the rejects got out" and insisting that "the shift" must be brought back. Kurt hotwires a forklift (Act Under Pressure 7, then 12 to drive it bent double, with Andrew's attempt to help failing on a 4) and rams the door open. The man returns with a bear-suit top, a face shield and a shotgun, and the team helps itself to more bear suits, shotguns, pepper spray, air horns and hockey masks. (Appalachia 09)

Jan's one condition for the job, the man says, was "don't ask questions about the ape-men." There is a great deal of gold left under Dahlonega, and ape-men dig it because they do not talk. A shift is twenty-five of them. They arrive looking about six years old and are full-grown in two months; they are trained with clickers and kept on ketamine. The operation has run for a year and a half, and Jan "kept getting more". The handler has been underground for two months training the new shift and does not know about the missing children. (Appalachia 09)

The conspiracy, he explains later in the gold room, was five people, "the biggest conspiracy you could possibly keep": Jan, the handler, two bodyguards, and a mercenary who melted the gold down. Kurt tells him about the dead man in the Bigfoot costume with military tattoos, and the handler recognises the scheme at once: "God damn it, he did the Bigfoot thing. Did he use the Chewbacca costume?" The dead man was the mercenary. The fake sightings were meant to discredit real sightings of escaped workers, whom Jan claimed the mercenary had "put down". Kurt assumes Jan killed the mercenary; nobody confirms it. The forklift cannot reach the elevator shutter's release, 25 feet up, so the plan becomes: drug the shift, and leave through the mines. (Appalachia 09)

docs.title: Gold and the crack in the air
docs.text:
The mine elevator is already at the bottom, empty. In the gold room a kitchen table holds hundreds of pounds of cast bars, and the handler sees that about half of the gold is missing. Everyone takes some under the banner of "civil forfeiture": Huell and the Biz take enough to earn -1 forward on physical rolls, Kurt a reasonable amount "for my wife and kids", Andrew about six bars in his satchel, and the sheriff a few to "figure out the legality later". (Appalachia 09)

In the narrowing tunnels they hear hissing. A side tunnel is lit by rippling light around a hard-edged crack in the air, with a metal pipe passing through it and venting gas. Through it are faint industrial machinery and darkness. The gas makes voices high-pitched; Kurt guesses hydrogen and bans gunfire and sparks. The handler says that as far as he knows Jan does not have a portal. Kurt: "Somebody fucking does." Andrew's camera being broken, the Biz photographs the crack with his spy camera on a timer, his fingers going electric and freezing as he reaches near it. Only after this does the handler give his name: Clive. (Appalachia 09)

docs.title: The shift
docs.text:
Around a corner, eyes reflect in the dark. The working shift of ape-men, in hi-vis vests and safety helmets, with pickaxes and blinking red tracking armbands, blocks the only exit, and the treats Clive has put down for them are not drugged. Preparedness rolls turn up Corn Nuts and Combos; the team guts the Combos and refills them with ketamine paste. Something growls behind them. Clive says that is Big Bob, and that they must run once they are past. (Appalachia 09)

Kurt walks out, eats a spiked Combo, mimes ecstasy and gets genuinely high. On a Manipulate Someone of 11 the ape-men lunge, see his face relax, and understand. They spoon ketamine into their mouths; one hugs him and another hands him a jackhammer. The team squeezes past and runs. (Appalachia 09)

docs.title: Big Bob
docs.text:
Something fast is twenty feet behind and gaining. Kurt calls a shotgun volley on three. Nobody rolls a full success, and Andre's rolls for the sheriff (6) and Clive (7) are no better. Andrew, who has dropped to the rear to shield Huell, is swung by the ankle into a wall for 4 harm, cracking his helmet and dislocating his knee; Big Bob then throws Kurt into the Biz. In the second round Kurt rolls 11 and puts a shot into its chest that should be fatal, but it keeps coming on adrenaline, cracks one of Kurt's ribs and lifts and crushes Huell. Andrew rolls Kick Some Ass for 10 and uses the "absence" of his pepper spray to sever the arm. Big Bob looks at the stump and topples over dead. Andrew keeps the hand. (Appalachia 09)

Four corners later, Clive brings them to a ladder under a tarp. Andrew and Huell each climb on an 8 and cannot walk afterwards. They emerge in the woods outside the plant. The unguarded ladder explains the escapes: the handlers relied on the ape-men's fear of dark tunnels. Kurt worries that the gas will blow the mine. The sheriff hugs a tree and sways. (Appalachia 09)

docs.title: Cold open and framing
docs.text: The cold open follows Jan. He steps out of an elevator, snaps "Not now, Marlene" at his secretary when she mentions the waiting reporters, and goes through to the parking garage. He unlocks a service lift, drags out a large animal crate on a dolly, loads it into a red pickup, and drives out the back onto the highway. "And we cut to credits." There is no "previously on"; Zack asks Andre for a recap. Ben joined the call to listen and asked one rules question. See the show. (Appalachia 09)

docs.title: Revelations
docs.text:
• Jan Martense ran an illegal gold mine under Dahlonega with ape-man labor. Clive says Jan insisted on at least a hundred million dollars; Clive would have settled for one or two.
  • The ape-men mature in about two months, are kept on ketamine, and are contained mainly by their fear of unlit tunnels.
  • The man in the Chewbacca costume was the conspiracy's mercenary, and the Bigfoot hoax was cover for real escapes through an unguarded ladder.
  • Someone with technology far beyond Spud Hut's has opened a rift into the mine and is piping gas through it.
  • The ape-men have an adrenaline gland "about twice the size of your fist", which is how Big Bob kept going.
  • Clive was never allowed into one room, which held an ape-man he knew of only from the food sent to it.

(Appalachia 09)

docs.title: Table notes
docs.text:
• The jawbone in Huell's backside, and his worry about becoming a were-ape. See running gags.
  • Andre points out that the "break room" of Appalachia 08 "was never a break room. It was just a door", and the Claymore has blown the door away; Dante calls it "a broke room".
  • The Biz's missing night-vision goggles come up again; he plans to buy a new pair with gold.
  • Dante predicted Clive's plan had "too many steps", and was right.
  • Dice: Dante rolled 11 at each moment that mattered (quieting the sheriff, the ketamine pantomime, the shot that killed Big Bob); Rita's Help Out on the forklift failed on a 4. See game mechanics.
  • Andre called Big Bob "Big Bill" once and corrected himself. Nobody asked the handler's name until after the portal; until then Andre called him "the man with no name".
  • Dante complained that Jan's name kept changing between "Jan" and "Yan"; Andre's answer was that people in town do not say it correctly.

(Appalachia 09)

docs.title: Continuity
docs.text:
• Continues directly from the cliffhanger of Appalachia 08.
  • The Claymore's toll changes between episodes. At the end of Appalachia 08 Andre counted one creature dead and at least two badly injured. In this episode his recap says the mine "evaporated two", and the team tells Clive that two of the five rejects are dead.
  • Clive's account of the mercenary explains the body in Appalachia 06 and the Chewbacca figure Monica Cartwright described in Appalachia 04.
  • The Biz cannot find his night-vision goggles, last seen in the hands of the state police in the cold open of Appalachia 06.
  • The shift's blinking armbands match the tracking device the Circle Chasers found in Appalachia 07.
  • The arc's finale, Appalachia 10, was never recorded. The recorded story stops with the team injured in the woods and Jan at large.

(Appalachia 09)

docs.title: The Things in Appalachia, Episode 10
docs.text:
The finale of the arc, in which the team caught up with Jan Martense and the Spud Hut plant exploded, was played but never recorded.

Arc The Things in Appalachia Episode 10 (unrecorded finale) Setting The woods and mines around the Spud Hut plant, Dahlonega, Georgia In-fiction date October 1992, the same day as Appalachia 08 and 09 Previous Appalachia 09 Next Walkers 01

Unrecorded session

This session was played but never recorded. What happened in it is known only from what the characters and players say in the next recorded session, Walkers 01: Kurt's interrogation of Jan, the Biz's appearance on Late Night with David Letterman, and the conversation at the table around them. See lost episodes.

docs.title: Where Episode 09 leaves off
docs.text: Appalachia 09 ends with the team in the woods outside the plant, at the top of a ladder out of the mines. Huell Kendrick and Andrew Howard can no longer walk, Kurt Larson has a cracked rib and a dose of ketamine in him, and everyone is carrying gold bars. Sheriff Carter Burke and the animal handler Clive are with them. Jan Martense has driven out of the plant in a red pickup with a large animal crate, about half the gold is missing, and a crack in the air is venting gas into the tunnels. (Appalachia 09)

docs.title: The confrontation with Jan
docs.text:
• Jan shot Andrew in the face. When Jan greets Kurt with "Kurtis, you shot me", Kurt answers, "Ah, you shot my leader in the face. Seemed only fair." Jan remarks that Andrew "recovered from that remarkably well".
  • Kurt shot Jan.
  • The Biz also fired on him. On Letterman he jokes about "shooting a Polish person", and Ezra spells it out at the table: "I shot a Polish man in the woods with a shotgun."
  • Jan was then crushed by a falling ape-man, which broke his skull, and he almost bled to death.
  • Jan had meant the team to die underground. "I mean, you were intended to die, so, you know." He is still puzzled that the ape-men did not kill them.
  • Kurt assumes that Jan had already "taken care of" his mercenary in the woods, and Jan does not contradict him.

(Walkers 01)

docs.title: Shelly
docs.text:
Kurt questions Jan about an ape woman Jan called Shelly, describing Jan as the only person besides the handler who saw her alive "while not trying to kill you for any duration of time". The team therefore met Shelly in the finale, and she attacked them. (Walkers 01)

Jan's account of her is the origin of the ape-men. Five years earlier, driving drunk, he struck and killed a man in a black suit who was crossing a Georgia highway at night. The man carried NSA identification, and in his van was an ape woman strapped to a gurney and being fed drugs. Jan sank the body in a lake in the man's own vehicle and kept her. She was aging quickly, so he set out to breed from her; the ape-men are her sons by Jan himself, the female offspring not having lived. To Jan she "seemed like a bright chimp", unusual only for her voice mimicry. (Walkers 01)

docs.title: The explosion
docs.text: The Spud Hut facility exploded shortly after Jan fled it, on the same day as everything else. Kurt tells Jan that "some other force" filled the mines with explosive gas, probably from an adjacent cavern, and that the timing implies someone who knew the operation was ending. Jan has no idea who. Kurt does not tell him about the portal. (Walkers 01)

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text:
• Jan survived, was turned over to "the national security people" while he recovered, and is held at the CIA's Black Site Omaha, where Kurt interrogates him. He names one more person who knew about the mine: Clyde Harvard, an accountant at Spud Hut.
  • Clive survived the day. Kurt credits him with getting the team through the mines and passes on that he called Jan "the best boss he ever had", up to the point Jan tried to kill him.
  • Andrew spent about half as long in hospital as his doctors expected. Andre confirms that being shot in the face, juggled and slammed into cave walls all happened to him on the same day.
  • Kurt saw to it that the Spud Hut counter savant got a job at the CIA "in the wake of his job disappearing".
  • The Clinton surveillance scandal outlived the case. A month later the Biz goes on Letterman as "the most hated cop in America". The state police say they found his night-vision goggles in a rose bush, Polaroids of Bill Clinton taken with a Russian camera have become public, and the line the Biz is given is that "Jan Martense, the illegal gold miner for the food company" was the one surveilling Clinton.
  • President George H. W. Bush calls the affair "the debacle in Georgia" and puts the scandal down to "enemy action".

(Walkers 01)

docs.title: Unresolved
docs.text: No later episode says where Jan was caught, what was in the crate, or what became of the pickup and the missing gold. It is never stated whether the ape-man that fell on Jan was Shelly, or whether she survived. Sheriff Burke, the gold the team carried out, the drugged shift and the loose "rejects" are not mentioned again, and nobody says whether anyone was inside the plant when it exploded. Whoever opened the crack in the air and piped in the gas is carried forward as an unresolved mystery.

docs.title: Continuity
docs.text:
• Resolves the cliffhanger of Appalachia 09 and closes the arc.
  • Walkers 01 picks up a few weeks later with Andrew's meeting in the Oval Office, Kurt's interrogation of Jan and the Biz's appearance with David Letterman, before the briefing that sends the team to Utah.
  • Jan's hit-and-run victim gives the NSA a second dead man in black, after Agent Murphy in The Radford Horror; Dante remarks on it during the interrogation.

docs.title: The Walkers in Skin
docs.text:
The Walkers in Skin is the fourth canon arc of PITF, in which the task force goes to a haunted ranch in Utah to exhume a dead woman and finds two towns being replaced person by person.

Setting Washington, DC (episode 01); Sherman Ranch, Ballard and Roosevelt, Utah Episodes 9 recorded (01–09), plus one unrecorded session ("08.5") In-fiction dates Early November 1992, around Election Day (November 3) Main threat The skinwalkers: pilot organisms in manufactured copies of people Preceded by The Things in Appalachia (and the non-canon one-shot Philosopher's Fist) Followed by The Roulet Estate

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The arc opens with an epilogue to the Georgia case. With the Clinton surveillance scandal dominating the last days of the 1992 campaign, the Biz is sent onto David Letterman's show, President Bush tells Andrew Howard that the affair was enemy action, and Kurt Larson questions Jan Martense in a CIA black site. Then Alberta Wilmarth asks Andrew to dig up her mother, Shelly Wilmarth, who died in 1990 and has been seen alive. (Walkers 01)

In Utah the team lodges in a double-wide on Alberta's ranch, which she rents to the UFO-hunting billionaire Robert Bigelow. The first half of the arc is a slow accumulation of the strange: a coyote that walks upright, a car dragged sideways at dusk and later lifted into the sky and dropped flat in the next town, a night of hallucinations and levitation under a white ring, a cavern under the whole property, and a town government building a community center in the desert for no good reason. The comedy runs alongside, most of it supplied by Nancy the goose. (Walkers 02, Walkers 03, Walkers 04, Walkers 05)

The cold opens, which the characters never see, tell the audience the rest in advance: rows of bodies wrapped in plastic, a man feeding on Jell-O through gray tendrils, coyotes fed sugar by hand. In the second half the team catches up. Ballard's City Hall is abandoned and stocked with sugar, half the high school is missing, and the sheriff flees the state. (Walkers 06)

The turn comes in the school gym, where Andrew meets a copy of himself, fights it and loses. Andre runs the scene with the other three players out of the call, and at its end tells Rita that she is now playing the replica: a hurried, flawed clone that works for the enemy and passes itself off to the team as Andrew. (Walkers 07)

An autopsy by Donald McManley explains what the townspeople have become: engineered bodies steered by a pilot in the skull, living on blood and sugar. Roosevelt's police are massacred and impersonated, every car is stolen, and the road out is blockaded. In a session that was played but never recorded, the team reaches the National Guard by radio and retakes the Roosevelt police station. (Walkers 08, Walkers 08.5)

The finale is an assault on the community center with Guardsmen, horses and a homemade killdozer. The real Andrew, who died and came back as something else, returns to expose his double, and the team destroys a portal through which the skinwalkers were evacuating. (Walkers 09)

docs.title: The two Andrews
docs.text:
Rita plays two different characters under Andrew Howard's name in this arc, and for three sessions the rest of the table is not told.

Episodes Who Rita plays What the other players know Walkers 01 to the gym fight in Walkers 07 The real Andrew Howard. A dream of a naked double in Walkers 06 is the only warning. Everything; there is no secret yet. End of the gym scene in Walkers 07, Walkers 08, Walkers 08.5, first half of Walkers 09 The replica, the same double Andrew fought in the gym. Nothing. Dante, Ezra and Zack were out of the call for the gym scene and for Andre's briefing of Rita, and had left before the closing scene of Walkers 08, in which the real Andrew revives in the morgue as the Monstrous. Second half of Walkers 09 The real Andrew again, now the Monstrous. Andre takes over the replica. The real Andrew's arrival exposes the replica in front of everyone, and Andre announces, "Now that the game is up, Rita, let's swap back who we're controlling."

(Walkers 07, Walkers 08, Walkers 09)

docs.title: Episodes
docs.text: Episode Summary Walkers 01 Letterman, the Oval Office and a black site close out the Georgia case; Alberta Wilmarth brings a new one. Walkers 02 The team flies to Utah and meets Walt, Alberta, Bigelow and the goose at Sherman Ranch. Walkers 03 An electrical event drags the car at dusk; the sheriff, the bartender, the grave and the substation. Walkers 04 An upright coyote, a burned crow, two stoned teenagers, and a car that vanishes upward and returns flat. Walkers 05 The night event puts Andrew in the refrigerator and takes the Biz's fillings; radar finds a cavern. Walkers 06 A false confession, a fridge of sugar, a fleeing sheriff, a note, and a beam that launches sheet metal. Walkers 07 A naked intruder, upright horses in the gym, and Andrew replaced by his double. Walkers 08 Roosevelt cut off; the autopsy reveals pilots and vehicles; the real Andrew wakes in the morgue. Walkers 08.5 Played but never recorded. Horses, the radio station, the National Guard, and the police station retaken. Walkers 09 The killdozer assault, two Howards, and the portal under the community center.

docs.title: How it ended
docs.text: With the substation destroyed, the power to the cavern fails and the portal falters. Huell's grenade finishes the machine, stranding fifty or sixty skinwalkers in the dark, and the cavern and the community center above it collapse into a sinkhole. Andrew shoots his replica, whose pilot crawls out of its mouth and escapes. Above ground, everyone has been knocked out by a white powder falling from the sky while black triangular craft circle and hazmat crews remove the bodies. Kurt reports by radio that a cover-up the team did not cause is under way, and the team drives for a hospital with McManley, Walt and the surviving Guardsmen. On the radio, Ross Perot has won the presidency. (Walkers 09)

docs.title: Left unresolved
docs.text:
• Who operates the black triangles and the hazmat teams. (Walkers 09)
  • Where the portal led, who built the host bodies, and what became of the skinwalkers who got through, the mayor among them. (Walkers 08, Walkers 09)
  • What Andrew is now, and why he came back. (Walkers 08, Walkers 09)
  • What causes the ranch phenomenon, and who was switching the beam on and off. (Walkers 06, Walkers 09)
  • The exhumation of Shelly Wilmarth. The radar showed something solid in the coffin, and no recorded episode shows the grave opened. (Walkers 06)
  • Who wrote the "angels" note, and who paged Huell. (Walkers 06, Walkers 07)
  • From the epilogue: the dead man with NSA identification, the lake holding his car, and who piped gas into the Georgia mine. (Walkers 01)
  • The fates of Ned Simpson and the major. (Walkers 09)

See also Unresolved mysteries.

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text:
• Dates. The episodes do not quite agree on the calendar. Walkers 01 sets the Letterman taping on November 1, 1992, and the flight to Utah on "the day before the election". In Walkers 03, the team's first evening in Utah, Andre says it is "late October" and Ezra looks up the sunset for October 30. In Walkers 05 Andre says "tomorrow is the election", and Walkers 07 crosses midnight into November 3, Election Day. (Walkers 01, Walkers 03, Walkers 05, Walkers 07)
  • Shelly Wilmarth's death. Alberta says her mother died two years ago and shows an obituary dated winter 1990. When Rita asks in Walkers 05, Andre answers "about, I think, like two months ago". (Walkers 01, Walkers 05)
  • The unrecorded session. "Walkers 08.5" was played between episodes 08 and 09 but never recorded; what happened in it is known from the recap and references in Walkers 09. See its page and Lost episodes.

docs.title: The Walkers in Skin, Episode 01
docs.text:
The epilogue to the Georgia case: the Biz goes on Late Night with David Letterman, President Bush gives Andrew a private charge, Kurt questions Jan Martense in a CIA black site, and a woman asks the task force to dig up her mother.

Arc The Walkers in Skin Episode 01 (also the epilogue to The Things in Appalachia) Setting Washington, DC; New York City; CIA black site "Omaha" In-fiction date Early November 1992, in the last days before the presidential election Players present Andre (GM), Rita, Dante, Ezra, Zack; Ben listening in as a guest Previous Appalachia 10 (unrecorded) Next Walkers 02

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: A few days before the 1992 election, the Dahlonega case has become a national scandal. Dick "The Biz" Baxter, now "the most hated cop in America", is ordered onto David Letterman's show with Huell Kendrick in reserve, and burns a Luck point to win the host over. Andrew Howard is told by President George H. W. Bush that he is personally responsible for the survival of the United States. Kurt Larson interviews the captured Jan Martense under the ocean. Back in DC, Alberta Wilmarth knocks on Andrew's door: her mother died in 1990 and has been seen alive since. The trip to Utah is approved. (Walkers 01)

docs.title: The Oval Office
docs.text:
Andrew waits an hour and a half outside the Oval Office while the president's secretary glares at him. Digging in his satchel he finds a handful of Yeti fur he forgot to turn in, and drops a still-bloody clump on the carpet as he is called in. Bush, sitting on his desk, quotes the after-action report (a colleague wrote that Andrew was "dribbled like a basketball") and tells him "You're sturdy, son." (Walkers 01)

Bush admits he founded the task force only because his son made him promise to look into such things. Having read the files, he thinks Andrew is its only true believer; the others have a "grudging appreciation". Asked why he believed beforehand, Andrew answers that his mom believes and that he was never proven wrong. (Walkers 01)

Bush expects to lose within days. He regards an ape-man criminal surveilling Bill Clinton in the same Georgia town as his task force as enemy action, meant to break continuity of leadership. The source could be China, Soviet remnants, or "something from somewhere else". He warns of enemy agents inside American organizations and charges Andrew with the nation's survival whatever the next administration says. Andrew replies that this has always been his job and delivers a long lecture on the Aetherius Society, the Masters and the "spiritual battery". Bush's face goes blank in a slow zoom. (Walkers 01)

docs.title: Black site Omaha
docs.text:
Kurt passes through a naval research base and rides an elevator five stories under the sea to Black Site Omaha, run by the CIA. He pays the desk guard in ordinary cigarettes and is cleared for four hours. Jan is in a gray jumpsuit and plastic cuffs, stitched and bruised where a falling ape broke his skull. The two trade jabs ("Kurtis, you shot me." / "Ah, you shot my leader in the face. Seemed only fair.") and agree to a quid pro quo. Jan complains that prisoners are not allowed playing cards, and Kurt tells him how to make a deck out of napkins or coasters. (Walkers 01)

Jan's story: five years ago, driving drunk in the Georgia countryside, he hit and killed a man in a black suit who was crossing the highway at night. The dead man carried NSA identification. Jan sank the body in a lake in the man's car, and in the man's van found an ape woman strapped to a gurney and drugged. He took her and named her Shelly. She aged fast, and Jan could not go public with her, so he tried to breed her to buy time. When no ape donor worked he fathered her offspring himself by artificial insemination. Only the males lived. These were the ape-men, who mined gold for Jan's conspiracy because they were strong and could recognize it. (Walkers 01)

Jan does not know why the Spud Hut distribution center exploded. Kurt tells him the gas was piped in deliberately from an adjacent cavern, but keeps the portal to himself. The only other insider Jan names is the Spud Hut accountant, Clyde Harvard. Jan also says he bought his ketamine from a local high schooler. Kurt gets the name of the lake and, on the way out, promises to put in a word with the desk guard about anti-suicide playing cards. In the weeks since Georgia he has placed the Spud Hut savant in a CIA job, spent time with his family, and sourced a P90. (Walkers 01)

docs.title: Late Night
docs.text:
The FBI wanted a PR officer on the talk-show circuit; every show wanted someone actually involved, so the Biz was the concession. In makeup he is told "Stop sweating" and has a deodorant stick rubbed into his scalp. Huell, waiting backstage, is handed a ginger ale he did not ask for and drinks it. Ezra spends two stored level-ups here: the Charlatan move, and advanced Investigate a Mystery and Manipulate Someone. (Walkers 01)

Letterman brings Huell out for support and forgets his surname. The Biz opens with a joke about shooting a Polish person; Huell asks whether the culture has forgotten Rodney King. The audience reaction is "complicated". Asked why they were in Dahlonega, the Biz says he was having an affair with Bill Clinton, then that he can't say. Andre calls for Manipulate Someone at -2. The Biz burns a Luck point to make the result a 12, and picks Letterman, not the audience, as his ally for the rest of the mystery. The host drops his script and simply talks to him. (Walkers 01)

On air the unit is the invented "Foreign Threat Investigation Task Force". The Biz says 90% of its cases are nothing, swears, confirms the illegal gold mine and the same-day explosion, and says nobody knew Clinton was in town. On why Jan was surveilling the governor: "Maybe he's a Republican." The Georgia State Police found the Biz's night-vision goggles in a rose bush; he says they were last in his car trunk and he wants them back. Letterman reveals that the Clinton Polaroids were taken with a Russian camera, which is news to the Biz. He closes with a marked-card trick using his wallet and badge (Act Under Pressure, a 10): more claps than boos. A PA slips him Letterman's personal number. (Walkers 01)

docs.title: A dead woman in Utah
docs.text:
The next day at the office Andrew, healed in half the expected time, is finishing the Georgia paperwork alone. Diane gives Huell pogs and asks what to do about the "crazy people" dropping by, including a woman whose dead mother is haunting her. Andrew: "Ghosts aren't real." They agree on a tip box. A nuisance called Chester is "getting really aggressive"; Huell has been using Kurt's shovel on him. (Walkers 01)

That evening Alberta Wilmarth arrives at Andrew's apartment with a box of documents and tapes and one request: "I need you to force the Mormon church to exhume my mom." Shelly Wilmarth died of a heart attack in winter 1990, alone with the cattle. Yet she appears in local news footage of a community-center protest, and the tenant of the family ranch, "the space guy" (Robert Bigelow), has seen her walking the property line at night. Alberta calls the ranch cursed: boiled cattle, missing pets, lights in the sky, Navy men measuring radiation. Andrew rules out a twin, puts "doppelganger" back on the list, feeds her leftovers and keeps the box. (Walkers 01)

He phones Huell, who is playing Ms. Pac-Man in a bar, to ask whether Mormons can come back from the dead. The next morning, the day before the election, a stressed Big Bill approves the trip and the airfare. Andrew asks the team who wants to exhume a dead woman. Ross Perot is polling above 45%. (Walkers 01)

docs.title: Cold open and framing
docs.text: The episode opens on a wood-paneled tube TV on the floor of an empty, decaying room, water-light rippling on peeling green wallpaper. The set clunks on, zooms through the solar system to New York, and plays the Late Night intro (Gary Oldman on Dracula, musical guest Patti Smith, and "the most hated cop in America"). Someone breathes heavily behind the camera. Credits follow. The session intercuts three storylines, with a flashback "about an hour earlier" to the makeup chairs, and ends on a title card for the new arc; the players identify the destination as Skinwalker Ranch, and Andre confirms only "It's in Utah." See The show. (Walkers 01)

docs.title: Revelations
docs.text:
• The task force exists because Bush's son asked for it. (Walkers 01)
  • The ape woman came from the van of a man with NSA identification, killed on a road at night five years earlier. The players link him to the earlier man in black with the flame flashlight, also hit by a car. (Walkers 01)
  • The Spud Hut explosion was deliberate: someone piped gas in and knew the timing. (Walkers 01)
  • The Polaroids in the Clinton surveillance scandal were taken with a Russian camera. (Walkers 01)
  • The Biz tells the audience he is "already estranged from my wife"; Andre sums up what the public learned about him as "he's divorced". (Walkers 01)

docs.text:

  • Bush's warning of infiltrators, with the election a day away. (Walkers 01)

docs.title: Table notes
docs.text:
• "Ghosts aren't real" is Andrew's catchphrase. Zack calls it a long-running gag and "a callback to our last campaign". (Walkers 01)
  • The Luck trade: Manipulate Someone at -2 became a 12, and Ezra judged it "worth the luck point". See Game mechanics. (Walkers 01)
  • Dante, out of character: "I want a fucking P90." (Walkers 01)
  • Zack fact-checks Bush's real approval rating and the date of Netscape; Ezra looks up the price of a PVS-7 monocular (about $4,500). (Walkers 01)
  • Andre forgot the background music for an hour, and says the Jan interview runs "quick for dramatic purposes, not for in-universe purposes". (Walkers 01)

docs.title: Continuity
docs.text:
Unrecorded session

The Appalachia finale was never recorded. This episode does not recap it; what is known of how that case ended comes from passing dialogue here. See Appalachia 10 and Lost episodes.

  • What the dialogue establishes about the unrecorded finale: Kurt shot Jan; Jan shot Andrew in the face ("you shot my leader in the face"); a falling ape broke Jan's skull; Andrew was thrown around the mine by the foot; the Biz shot a Polish man in the woods with a shotgun; Jan tried to have his animal handler killed. (Walkers 01)
  • The man in the black suit hit on a road at night echoes Agent Murphy, the NSA man the team themselves ran down in Radford Horror 03. Dante makes the connection at the table. (Walkers 01)
  • Andre dates the Letterman interview to November 1, 1992. The office scene is "the following day" and the briefing is the morning after that, which Andre calls "the day before the election"; the real election was on November 3, so the episode's days do not quite add up. (Walkers 01)
  • Alberta says her mother died two years ago, and the obituary gives winter 1990. Walkers 05 contradicts this. (Walkers 01)
  • Sets up the whole Utah arc: the ranch, the "space guy", the Navy investigators and the exhumation. Letterman remains the Biz's ally. (Walkers 01)

docs.title: The Walkers in Skin, Episode 02
docs.text:
The task force flies to Utah, is briefed by the Salt Lake City FBI office, and moves into a double-wide on Sherman Ranch, where it meets a gate guard, a goose and a billionaire.

Arc The Walkers in Skin Episode 02 Setting Salt Lake City; Ballard, Utah; Sherman Ranch In-fiction date Shortly before the 1992 presidential election (one day, noon to evening); on the exact date see Walkers 03 Players present Andre (GM), Rita, Dante, Ezra, Zack; Ben as a guest Previous Walkers 01 Next Walkers 03

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: With Big Bill glad to have them far from any camera, the team flies to Salt Lake City and collects a case file from two local FBI agents who blame the ranch reports on lightning and drink. At Sherman Ranch they meet the gate guard Walt, their client Alberta Wilmarth, her goose Nancy, and the tenant Robert Bigelow, whose instruments record heat and electrical anomalies that stop half a mile from the ranch. A grocery run into Ballard turns up resentment of the town's leaders and their new community center. (Walkers 02)

docs.title: Out of the public eye
docs.text: Big Bill, distracted by the election, sets one condition: stop at the FBI Salt Lake City field office for the files on earlier reports and work with the local agents. The team flies, which costs Kurt Larson his Claymores but not his licensed P90. Andrew Howard books the rental, a 1990 Plymouth Voyager with fake-wood paneling. Dante's 2d6 flight roll is a six: a toddler kicks the seat of the Biz every 25 seconds, and a few passengers double-take at one of America's most hated people. (Walkers 02)

docs.title: The Salt Lake City briefing
docs.text:
In a second-floor conference room the team meets Carl Gardner, short, hearty and full of "big cop energy", and his tall, silent partner Philip Bishop. Kurt introduces himself as CIA, UTAW division; Gardner knows "those boys, explode the cigars and all that." Gardner's rundown of the ranch: a Native American former Army Ranger on the billionaire's security staff says he shot a snooper by the barn, though Gardner found no physical evidence; a young woman reports seeing her dead mother, and there is no twin; cattle mutilations, put down to lightning; lights and lost time, put down to drinking. (Walkers 02)

Kurt rolls Investigate a Mystery on the room's string-covered corkboard and gets a 9. The board is another case entirely: unacceptable levels of semen in public drinking fountains, the start of the Ballard water contamination thread. While Gardner goes to look up the billionaire's name, Huell Kendrick tries "So— Mormons, am I right?" on Bishop, and four minutes of sweaty silence follow. Gardner returns with the name of the billionaire who "skeeves me the hell out": Robert Bigelow, a real estate baron whose security man fired the shot. He hands over a copy of the file, recognizes the Biz as "the fella who spied on Clinton" ("Had it coming"), recommends funeral potatoes, and tells them to say they are "a friend of Bonaparte" for 20% off gas. Rita tests whether Andrew's appearance alone earns the discount; the receipt shows it did. (Walkers 02)

docs.title: Sherman Ranch
docs.text:
After a drive of almost three hours the team reaches Ballard, a town of a few hundred with a sheriff's station in a double-wide, and then the ranch gate. Walt, the guard, is the man who fired at the snooper: he says he gave a warning first and the figure came at him "at pretty high speed". He came back from the Gulf War about a year ago. He asks whether they have come about "the sugar heist", a box truck of cane sugar stolen from a truck stop three or four weeks ago. He calls the ranch "haunted as hell": sheep that burst ("You ever microwaved an egg?"), cattle simply dead (see livestock mutilations). (Walkers 02)

Walt leads them to the guest double-wide and is promptly attacked and bitten by Nancy, an enormous goose. He explains the house (furnace on a switch, keys under a ceramic frog, a back door with only a deadbolt) and the rules: headlights on at night, and the big house and its barn are off-limits. From the window he points out the white community center and its gray substation, built four miles out of town and in sight of the ranch. Some of the town's leaders, he says, "make my skin crawl". (Walkers 02)

At the pig pen Alberta welcomes Andrew and admits she "genuinely did not expect to get traction". She makes Walt confess that in the summer of 1986 he tried to get people to call him "Coyote"; Andrew and Kurt adopt the name at once. Something pulled up a couple of fence posts overnight and Walt's dog was cagey, though the animal headcount was fine. Alberta has seen no lights, but the ranch always hums at night, which sets Andrew visibly vibrating. Nancy runs at Kurt at full speed, jumps into Alberta's arms and hisses at him. (Walkers 02)

docs.title: Bigelow
docs.text: At the big house a blonde guard with a ponytail and a hip holster, the Ponytail Lady, asks them to leave their weapons at the door. Kurt says no, so the meeting happens on the porch over sweet tea and buttered bread. Bigelow, a sour-faced middle-aged man in an expensive suit, calls Alberta "Madeline" and corrects himself. He has read up on the team ("a lot of interesting stories follow in your wake"), and the Clinton affair "didn't even make the list". His operation logs electromagnetic, thermal and acoustic readings on tape reels: many unexplained heat signatures and electrical events, all within the ranch and half a mile around it, none in town. He dismisses the substation as unrelated. He already knows about the contamination in Ballard's water and adds that it is high in arsenic; the big house filters its own. He stands by Walt's judgment over the shooting, is asked about the team joining a night patrol, and leaves for a satellite-phone call. The guard gives the house rules: keep Bigelow happy, and keep the goose happy. (Walkers 02)

docs.title: Ballard
docs.text: At the general store a lifelong resident with an enormous beehive hairdo sells them bologna, white bread and cheap beer for $35.25. Andrew's awkward questioning gets results anyway: the ranch is weird, "but that's the county"; she resents the community center, blames the mayor (Wilford Hiram) and "the goddamn busybody" Deborah Wells, and would rather have a clinic. The team tells her to drink only bottled or well water. On the drive back Kurt informs Andrew that he has no game. The night ends with Kurt taking the toddler's bedroom and test-flushing a toilet that gurgles long and anemically. (Walkers 02)

docs.title: Cold open and framing
docs.text: No player characters appear. At night on a desert ranch, a Native American man in a big cowboy hat arrives with a shotgun and a large dog, which growls softly into the dark. He finds nothing and drives off. A coyote steps out from behind the sheep, trots toward the edge of the pasture, and stands up on two legs. Cut to credits. Ezra: "Regular coyote." Andre: "Yeah, just normal." See upright coyotes and The show. (Walkers 02)

docs.title: The Walkers in Skin, Episode 03
docs.text:
On the team's first evening in Utah, something kills the rental car and drags it sideways at dusk, and a night in Ballard yields a sheriff, a bartender, an undisturbed grave and an overloaded substation.

Arc The Walkers in Skin Episode 03 Setting Sherman Ranch and Ballard, Utah In-fiction date Late October 1992 by Andre's account at the table, from about 5:30 p.m. into the night (see Continuity) Players present Andre (GM), Rita, Dante, Ezra, Zack Previous Walkers 02 Next Walkers 04

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: Heading into town to start the exhumation, the team is caught in the dusk event: the car dies fifty feet from the ranch gate, the sky pulses, and the van slides six inches sideways before everything returns to normal. In Ballard, Sheriff McDermish agrees to file the exhumation paperwork and the bartender Maggie supplies the town's gossip. The team finds Shelly Wilmarth's grave untouched, a substation arcing into the ground, and a fenced community center site with a clear view of their own front door. (Walkers 03)

docs.title: Ham bang
docs.text:
After a dinner of sandwiches and 3% beer in the guest double-wide, the team decides to go into town about an hour before sunset. Nancy the goose is waiting outside. Kurt Larson's flashbangs are in checked baggage, so Huell Kendrick throws lunch meat instead (Manipulate Someone, a flat 10). Halfway to the car the goose comes back for more. Huell's Act Under Pressure is an 8, a partial: everyone gets in, but she bites his nose until it bleeds and swells shut. (Walkers 03)

At the big house, Walt Murphy hands Andrew Howard an unrequested brownie and promises to clear a night-patrol ride-along with Bigelow and fetch them around 1 a.m. He warns them not to shoot the livestock, which "move in ways that look pretty odd if you're jumpy." Huell is paged by Donald McManley, who answers the return call with "Is it a real one this time?" He will not drive the RV to Utah; he needs warning to repack and fly. Huell promises to call the moment the case looks real. (Walkers 03)

docs.title: The dusk event
docs.text:
Fifty feet from the gate the Plymouth Voyager dies, and every electronic device in it with it. Outside there is a high, tinnitus-like whine; thin clouds flicker with lightning and the hair stands up on their necks. Kurt: "That's fucking lightning." They retreat into the car. The sky pulses brighter and dimmer in a stuttering rhythm while Andrew photographs it and Huell develops a pounding headache. Then the car moves six inches sideways, something pops, and the engine restarts. (Walkers 03)

Kurt runs UTAW-style checks: trash out the window, his non-dominant hand out the door, a taste of the air. Tire trails confirm the drag, and there is nowhere to hide a giant electromagnet. His battery watch has stopped, the two-dollar Casio worn by the Biz is permanently scrambled, and Andrew's mechanical Fossil is fine. Under the hood are four or five scattered scorch marks where the metal got hot enough to anneal. Andrew mutters about the 1950s Levelland, Texas case. Huell, told to call McManley, says "maybe later". (Walkers 03)

docs.title: The sheriff and the bartender
docs.text:
The door of the sheriff's double-wide is answered by seven-year-old Bud: "My daddy's on the shitter. Can I help you?" Sheriff McDermish, part-time, heavyset and eager to be "a resource", serves sweet tea beside a Monopoly game he is losing to his son. He will file the exhumation paperwork tomorrow, but warns that the judge once stalled an exhumation for six months. The team tells him not to drink the tap water; Bigelow had told him the same without saying why. (Walkers 03)

At the bar the young bartender takes Andrew for a "Mormon fed", demands ID, makes him drink a vodka-Coke shot, then softens and gives him a root beer float. Huell beats the Biz at darts by spending a Luck point on a 7; the Biz rolls a 4 and pays $20 on a bet nobody made. The bartender recognizes both of them from television. Her gossip: the community center is being built half a county away from the community, pushed by Deborah Wells, on Pueblo ruins that were bulldozed despite a protest. Ballard has about thirty blackouts a year, four school computers that never worked, and a stink at the high school; anyone who can get a degree "magically" disappears. She once saw something she took for ball lightning streak past her car on the ranch's back road and shoot straight up. (Walkers 03)

Drunk, Huell tells her about the water. The Biz coins "Half-Gallon Howard"; Andrew turns red and studies the counter. The sheriff trades Vietnam stories with Kurt and describes his shot-off buttock until the bartender bans both topic and display. She introduces herself only at the end: "I'm Maggie, by the way. Not that anyone asks." (Walkers 03)

docs.title: The grave, the substation, the site
docs.text:
Kurt picks the cheap lock on the churchyard cemetery. After half an hour they find Shelly Wilmarth's grave under an expensive black granite slab: undisturbed, tidy, with grass trampled by a recent visitor. (Walkers 03)

Near the ranch turnoff the substation is popping and flickering. Kurt's Investigate a Mystery is a 10, two questions: the equipment is arcing into the ground, it is being driven far harder than it was designed for, and something blew into it and made a path to ground. The community center itself is a cinder-block shell behind chain-link and barbed wire, with work lights on and "cultural genocide" painted over the contractor's logos. It stands at the end of a dirt road in empty desert, and the double-wide is visible from it. Kurt concludes the ranch is the likely reason it was built there. Back home a goose-shaped silhouette charges out of the dark and rattles the doorknob. (Walkers 03)

docs.title: Cold open and framing
docs.text: A slow zoom through a dark, dusty industrial space of wires and pipes, lit by thin shafts of light from below, with distant shouting. The camera passes row after row of human-shaped figures wrapped in clear plastic. As it reaches the last one, it moves. Cut to credits. These are the plastic-wrapped bodies. There is no "previously on". (Walkers 03)

docs.text:

Both episodes agree only that the election has not yet happened. (Walkers 03)
  • The sheriff points at a moth scar on Kurt's neck, and the Biz's let-down over the moth and Kurt's "off-brand Bigfoot" recall the Radford and Appalachia cases. The team's one large "sock full of gold", still sitting in the DC office, comes from Appalachia. (Walkers 03)
  • McManley's "Is it a real one this time?" follows his call-outs in The Summer Service and The Things in Appalachia; his RV stays home. (Walkers 03)

docs.title: The Walkers in Skin, Episode 04
docs.text:
A night patrol produces a coyote on two legs, a carbonized crow and two stoned teenagers; then the rental car vanishes straight upward and comes back flat in the next town.

Arc The Walkers in Skin Episode 04 Setting Sherman Ranch; Roosevelt, Utah In-fiction date The night after Walkers 03 and the following day Players present Andre (GM), Rita, Dante, Ezra, Zack Previous Walkers 03 Next Walkers 05

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: On the way to and during the 1 a.m. patrol, Kurt Larson is stalked by an upright coyote, Andrew Howard finds a crow burned to charcoal in the pig pen, and the team frightens two Ballard teenagers out of the barn. When they get back, the Plymouth Voyager is gone, with no tracks leaving. It turns up the next morning in Roosevelt, a foot thick and fused into the road. The team acquires a loaner squad car called Betsy, loses a jacket to the goose, wins the exhumation order through Big Bill, and orders ground-penetrating radar and a bomb collar. (Walkers 04)

docs.title: "Parlez-vous français?"
docs.text: With an hour to go before the patrol, Kurt walks to the big house to compare its instrument records with the substation pop and the car's sideways slide. A curt doorman says Bigelow is asleep. Walking back, Kurt realizes he is being followed. A Preparedness roll (8 on the dice, 11 with Sharp) puts a wad of baloney in his pocket. He throws it and turns: a coyote is standing on two legs, eyes glinting. He asks it "Parlez-vous français?" as a verbal flashbang. It stares, then runs, dropping to all fours as it speeds up. Nancy the goose scuttles out and takes the baloney. Soon afterwards the Voyager's alarm goes off with nothing near it. (Walkers 04)

docs.title: The patrol
docs.text:
Walt "Coyote" Murphy collects them in his Jeep and falls in love with Kurt's P90. Andrew, watching the sky, sees something small drop into the pig pen. His Investigate a Mystery is a 9: it is a crow burned to a crisp, feathers crumbling, eyes burst, bones cracked by heat. It fell with no sound and no flash. Walt suggests ball lightning; Andrew cites the 1957 Levelland case, and half an hour of UFO talk moves Walt from suspicion to grudging respect. The crow goes into a dog-waste bag for Donald McManley. (Walkers 04)

The Biz spots a figure with a glint near the barn. Kurt and Huell Kendrick go in through a loose chain; Kurt's Read a Bad Situation (9) finds two extremely stoned teenagers behind the equipment. The glint was a holographic snap bracelet. Walt recognizes Harrison; the silent one is Marshall Crichton. They came on a dare to look for ghosts or aliens. Harrison describes the tiny Ballard High School (about sixty students, an eye-watering smell this semester). Kurt confiscates their terrible weed, comes back with good weed, and a Manipulate Someone (10) scares Harrison into taking it. Walt: "You guys are the weirdest fucking cops I've ever met." (Walkers 04)

docs.title: The vanishing car
docs.text:
Back at the guest double-wide the Voyager is gone. One set of tire tracks leads in; none lead out. Huell's Investigate a Mystery is a 10: the car most likely went straight up, and the ground where it stood is about 200 degrees. Walt offers a junkyard magnet crane, a skyhook, a helicopter with a long cable, anything but "moon man talk". Around 3 a.m. Huell phones McManley ("I think there's aliens and shit. You should be over here") and hangs up. (Walkers 04)

About 10 a.m. Andrew's pager goes off. Hertz reports the car is blocking East Lagoon Street in Roosevelt. Andrew: "It got unabducted." At the big house the Ponytail Lady has cued the camera tape (Bigelow's recordings): a gray patch seems to rise, unconvincingly. Radar saw nothing, but the electromagnetic meters "went nuts", and the earlier substation pop and car slide match spikes too. Before they leave, Nancy gets into the double-wide and Huell shuts her inside (Act Under Pressure, a 12). The guard lends them dusty road bikes. Huell cannot ride one; double sixes on Act Under Pressure, even at -1, let him fake it for almost a mile and a half before he falls. This is the vanishing car. (Walkers 04)

docs.title: Roosevelt
docs.text: The Voyager is pancaked about a foot thick and fused into a slight crater in the roadway. Officer Hernandez of the Roosevelt Police Department assumes vandals with a roller crusher and will check junkyards. He waives the tickets after a glance at Andrew's ID and arranges a loaner: Betsy, an old squad car that makes cartoon putt-putt noises. Five officers with jacks and two-by-fours cannot lever the wreck free. Huell's Help Out is double sixes again, a 15, and he lifts it with his back; ten to twenty percent of the car stays in the asphalt. Kurt's stilts, which he had "since Vietnam", went with the car; Betsy's trunk holds Cats costumes and a replacement pair. (Walkers 04)

docs.title: Goose, judge and fixers
docs.text:
The goose is still shut in the double-wide. In "Operation Get Goose Out" she drops onto Andrew's head from above the door, and his pendant repels the first strike. Kurt pries her off with the stilts (a 9), and the price is that she escapes with Andrew's jacket. The house is wrecked. (Walkers 04)

Andrew spends hours on the phone over the exhumation. His Manipulate Someone (7) cannot move a judge with religious objections, so he calls Big Bill, who talks to the judge for twenty minutes; the judge calls back sounding shaken. The exhumation is set for the day after tomorrow. As a plan B, the Biz uses his Fixer move twice, rolling 12 both times. Drebin, a Salt Lake City dealer in search equipment and a friend of his ex-wife's brother (he is not named until Walkers 05), will rent them ground-penetrating radar for about $800 and deliver it tomorrow. Hooster, a DC informant on parole and "criminal MacGyver", agrees to build a bomb collar so long as no dog is involved, supply thermite, and sell a net gun for the goose. His price is an invitation to the policeman's ball and help with parking tickets. Andrew retires to the bathroom so as not to be part of the conversation. (Walkers 04)

docs.title: Cold open and framing
docs.text: A pale, morbidly obese man in a wife beater walks through the desert with a shovel to a trailer. He passes a large cross and a mirror in the entryway, takes something from the fridge and sits in a recliner. A human-shaped figure wrapped in something shiny is propped in the other chair. He lifts a plate of Jell-O to his chin, and fine gray tendrils spool out of his mouth onto it while his dead eyes watch the muted TV. "We cut to credits." The man is later identified as Doug. (Walkers 04)

docs.text:

  • Zack rolls double sixes twice (faking the bike ride, and the 15 that lifts the car), and Ezra gets 12 twice on Fixer ("I have plus three to Charm, though"). Huell's one failure, a 6 at the wreck, earns experience. See Game mechanics. (Walkers 04)
  • Zack rules, for humor, that Huell cannot ride a bicycle. (Walkers 04)
  • "We are not being very good with rentals lately." (Walkers 04)
  • Dante stops to ask whether Utah had a stand-your-ground law yet in the early 1990s. (Walkers 04)
  • Rita mishears East Lagoon Street as "the Goon". (Walkers 04)

docs.title: The Walkers in Skin, Episode 05
docs.text:
The team inspects the flattened car, lives through a night of private hallucinations that ends with Andrew floating out of a refrigerator, and finds a cavern under the whole ranch.

Arc The Walkers in Skin Episode 05 Setting Sherman Ranch; Roosevelt, Utah In-fiction date The afternoon after Walkers 04 through the next day; Andre says the election is "tomorrow" on the first afternoon Players present Andre (GM), Rita, Dante, Ezra, Zack Previous Walkers 04 Next Walkers 06

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: The wreck of the Plymouth Voyager turns out to be magnetized and to have hit the road sideways at terminal velocity. That night the night event strikes the guest double-wide: each agent hallucinates something different, Andrew Howard levitates, and the Biz loses every filling in his mouth. Robert Bigelow's sky camera has filmed a white ring. The next day the rented ground-penetrating radar finds a cavern seventy feet down, the mayor pays a call, and a junkyard owner confesses to crushing the car. (Walkers 05)

docs.title: The wreck
docs.text:
With nothing scheduled until tomorrow, the team drives Betsy to the Roosevelt police station. A young officer, starstruck when Kurt Larson admits to being CIA "on loan", is rewarded with the story of how Kurt accidentally exploded Fidel Castro's dog. The wreck lies on its side in the garage. Kurt tests it with loose screws: it is magnetic now, and was not when parked. His Best of Queen tape survived but plays only static. Andrew attacks the trunk with a crowbar (Kick Some Ass, 8), falls, and has the harm absorbed by his pendant. (Walkers 05)

Kurt's Investigate a Mystery ("only a six, but it's a nine") shows that all the damage came from hitting the ground at terminal velocity: the car was skewed in the direction away from the ranch, as if still moving that way when it fell, and landed upside down. The upholstery is slightly melted and it smells of coyote urine. Andrew: "Car got abducted. They didn't want it, though." Pressed by the Biz with a plastic FBI badge, the officer gives up the department's suspect, a local junkyard owner with a crusher, a magnetic crane, car-theft priors and no alibi. (Walkers 05)

At Stewart's grocery the checkout lady winks at "Half-Gallon Howard". Donald McManley pages Huell Kendrick: he is flying in tomorrow, having first thought the team said "ghosts". Andrew dictates a field-kit list of crystals, "energy batteries", tinfoil and microwave parts. (Walkers 05)

Back at the ranch, Alberta Wilmarth sits in her truck bed with Nancy calm in her lap. Told about the coyote that followed Kurt on two legs, she says it is "probably one of the weird ones", and that there is a reason she does not live here anymore. The team spends a couple of hours pounding in four posts and chaining Betsy to them. A single eye watches from the roof of the house; when they have backed fifty feet away, the goose drops from it. (Walkers 05)

docs.title: The night event
docs.text:
Huell wakes to screaming as the world pivots ninety degrees, like a tumble dryer, and Andrew's bed is empty. Kurt wakes in Saigon and shouts in Vietnamese from behind the dresser. The left half of the Biz's vision is outer space crumbling, and he tastes blood. Andrew is buried alive and freezing. (Walkers 05)

Huell traces the screaming to the refrigerator, but his Act Under Pressure, at -1, is a 6 and he crashes through the card table. Kurt's roll to remember his mission is a 7, a mixed result: part of him stays stuck in Saigon, so he bites his LSD tooth and shifts into a state that is still broken but more familiar. He opens the fridge, which to him is the trunk of an ancient tree. Andrew spills out flailing and floats toward the ceiling. Kurt hauls him down by the ankle as white light pours through the windows. (Walkers 05)

Then it stops, and everyone drops to the carpet. Every filling in the Biz's mouth is gone. Andrew had clawed the food and shelves out of the fridge before sealing himself inside. Guns, badges and wallets are scattered and the silverware is in a pile. The house has shifted a few inches, so that the stairs no longer line up with the porch, and it is warmer than the air outside. Bigelow phones to ask whether they saw a white light. Andrew is furious: "God damn it, I almost got abducted. Why weren't the windows open?" Kurt treats the Biz's mouth with cocaine from his shoe heel. (Walkers 05)

docs.title: The ring
docs.text: At the big house an exhausted Walt hands out coffee and cider. Bigelow shows a frozen frame from his sky camera (Bigelow's recordings): a bright white ring with a faint purple glow, oscillating for a few seconds. He talks about the Black Sun and quotes Revelation 6:12. A lot of his equipment broke and the thermal camera whited out. Betsy, chained outside, is untouched and cold. His staff have been having nightmares; one, Marina, dreams of drowning. The events have been escalating for weeks, and he thinks "we may be on the verge of making contact". Kurt offers a cover story about Russian neurological warfare and gets Bigelow to agree to ring the double-wide with cameras. Around 4 a.m. Rita asks when Alberta's mother died; Andre answers "about, I think, like two months ago", and Andrew lines the escalation up with Shelly Wilmarth's reappearance a few weeks back: "We really gotta dig that body up." (Walkers 05)

docs.title: The cavern and the mayor
docs.text:
In the morning a Roosevelt dentist working from a spare room refills the Biz's teeth in gold, the only material on hand, over five hours. Drebin delivers the radar with his iguana Herbert on his shoulder and demonstrates on the septic tank: an empty coffin would show a void, a full one would not. Then he notices a large signal seventy feet down, "like a cave". Kurt's Sharp roll is a 13: the cave extends under the whole area, with no shallower point on the property. Alberta, by phone, guesses a natural gas bed and asks them to tell no one until she works out "the play". (Walkers 05)

Mayor Wilford Hiram arrives in a new Cadillac. His rings cut Andrew's hand in the handshake. He crunches lemon candies from a tin throughout, fishes for why federal agents are in town, and leaves offering the help of "the government of Ballard, Utah". Andrew and Kurt give him the "oddball task force" cover and trust him not at all. (Walkers 05)

The Roosevelt officer phones: the junkyard owner (Yusuf Ansari) has confessed, with no motive given. Andrew tells the others, "I think the aliens coerced a guy into confessing." They collect the Biz, loopy on Novocain and nitrous, and go to interview him. (Walkers 05)

docs.title: Cold open and framing
docs.text: Andre opens with a spoken recap, then the cold open. A woman drives a pickup into the desert, one hand on a bulging backpack. Coyotes encircle the truck in the afternoon sun. One opens its mouth unsettlingly wide, gray fibers swimming up its throat. The backpack is full of white powder; she scoops it with a coffee cup and pours it down the coyote's throat. "And we cut to credits." (Walkers 05)

docs.text:

  • Andre says the election is "tomorrow" on this episode's first afternoon, the team's second day in Utah. Walkers 01 called the morning the team left Washington the day before the election, and Walkers 03 put their first evening in Utah in late October. (Walkers 05)

docs.title: The Walkers in Skin, Episode 06
docs.text:
The junkyard owner's confession falls apart, Ballard turns out to be emptying, City Hall has a refrigerator full of sugar, and something at the ranch fires sheet metal into the sky toward Roosevelt.

Arc The Walkers in Skin Episode 06 Setting Roosevelt, Utah; Ballard, Utah; Sherman Ranch In-fiction date 1992; one day, from about lunchtime to evening Players present Andre (GM), Rita, Dante, Ezra, Zack Previous Walkers 05 Next Walkers 07

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: Kurt Larson gets Yusuf Ansari to admit that he never touched the car and confessed under threat. The radar says there is something solid in Shelly Wilmarth's coffin. Ballard City Hall has been empty for days, and its padlocked fridge is stacked with sugar. Sheriff McDermish reports half the high school missing, hands Kurt a shotgun and leaves the state. Huell Kendrick is lured to a meeting that never happens and bitten by a stranger; Andrew Howard finds a note summoning him, alone, to the school gym at 1 a.m. At dusk the team discovers the beam. (Walkers 06)

docs.title: "I crush the car"
docs.text:
The team collects the Biz from the dentist, still numb. On the way Andrew suddenly remembers a dream from before he woke in the refrigerator: taking out the trash at his DC apartment, he found himself, naked, eating garbage, and the naked self chased him into the desert, smiling. (Walkers 06)

At the Roosevelt police station the interrogation room is also the lunchroom and smells of ham; a hungover officer named Carl microwaves Canadian bacon and says only "Ham." Yusuf Ansari, the junkyard owner, repeats "No immigration. I crush the car." He cannot say what kind of car it was, and agrees with whatever the Biz suggests. Kurt's Manipulate Someone is a 10. Yusuf admits he did nothing: his crusher cannot flatten a car that far, his magnetic crane does not move, and the police offered him a $10,000 fine and no immigration trouble if he confessed. His alibi is a half-hour landline call to his cousin and that night's Jeopardy!. Learning that Kurt is CIA, he groans, "Not the CIA. Not again." He agrees to owe the team a favor. Kurt phones Diane to have the call verified; she asks, "Any ape men?" (Walkers 06)

While this goes on, Huell is paged from an unknown number. A man's voice says he has something Huell should see about "your colleague": come to the grocery store in town in an hour, alone, to the little room in the back. (Walkers 06)

docs.title: The grave and City Hall
docs.text:
At the churchyard cemetery the ground-penetrating radar will not start, although Kurt follows the start-up instructions exactly (Act Under Pressure, 11). His Investigate a Mystery (10) finds thick wire bundles on the underside chewed through by teeth, in a spot that cannot be reached while the machine stands upright, as it had been left. Huell repairs it with gum-wrapper foil (double sixes, an 11 after modifiers). Over the grave the radar shows something solid in the coffin, at about 85% confidence. (Walkers 06)

Looking for survey records that might show an entrance to the cavern, the team walks to City Hall, a converted double-wide. As they approach, Huell's Read a Bad Situation is a 5: a growing dread he cannot place. Nobody answers. Kurt snaps a pick in the cheap lock (Act Under Pressure, 6, which marks experience and levels him up), fishes the broken end out on a second roll of 10, and shoulders the door. Inside, fans and a radio are running and everything is under dust. Nobody has been here for days. Huell finds the keys to a padlocked refrigerator: bags of coarse white granules stacked floor to ceiling. Kurt tastes it. It is sugar. Andrew's search (an 11) turns up a desk heaped with copies of the New York Post that stop abruptly about three months ago, buried in hundreds of Tootsie Roll wrappers. It is the mayor's desk; the other well-used one belongs to Deborah Wells. (Walkers 06)

Mayor Wilford Hiram's Cadillac pulls up. The team claims the door was open; the Biz's Manipulate Someone is a 7, and the mayor is cold and unconvinced. He says the geological records were lost in a fire, crunches lemon candies ("Special order. They're from Spain."), and locks up behind them. Huell's second Read a Bad Situation is double ones. Andrew proposes that the mayor has been replaced by a sugar-eating Scandinavian tooth troll. See sugar clues. (Walkers 06)

docs.title: The sheriff leaves
docs.text: Sheriff McDermish, chain-smoking on his porch, lays out the disappearances: a county spot-check found more than half the high school absent, while the school's own records show nothing; parents do not answer; houses have stood empty for days; the diner has three customers where there would usually be ten or fifteen. Most of the absent are Mormon. He gives Kurt a list of names and a Remington 870, then tells his son to get his backpack. From the sheriff's phone Kurt asks Big Bill to put the Utah National Guard on standby. Bill, already buried in "the political stuff", agrees and asks them not to need it. The sheriff, relieved that "the professionals are on it", drives off vowing not to stop until he is out of the state. (Walkers 06)

docs.title: The meeting that wasn't
docs.text: Huell borrows Kurt's P90 and goes to the general store alone; Andre removes the other players from the call. In the alley a ragged man asks for a dollar, then lunges. Huell's Kick Some Ass is double ones. The man bites his wrist, shouts "Pig!", takes the dollar and runs. The clerk bandages him and says, "we don't got homeless in Ballard." Huell searches the back room (Investigate a Mystery, 6) and waits half an hour. Nobody comes, and the pager number is unlisted. He walks back to the ranch. (Walkers 06)

docs.title: The note and the beam
docs.text:
At the double-wide Andrew shows the others a note he found in his bed. It says some of his friends "aren't who you think", that its writer knows he is not one of them because "you have angels", and that he should come to the school gym at 1 a.m. without the others. He decides to go; the team will drop him partway and wait within earshot. (Walkers 06)

A rattling draws them outside. A sheet of metal in the yard fence is shaking violently, with a faintly glowing vertical line through it. Huell pokes the line with a stick and lights a cigarette from it; his hand burns on both sides. A second sheet held over the line is ripped skyward. Huell's fourth Read a Bad Situation, an 11, shows dust hanging along a curved invisible arc with the clouds stretched along it. A penny is barely deflected; Kurt's broken watch rockets away. Their eyes begin to hurt. Kurt: "Guys, I think we're being microwaved." Then there is an electric pop and the dust falls. Andrew: "They just turned their thing off." The arc points toward town, in line with Roosevelt. (Walkers 06)

docs.title: Cold open and framing
docs.text: A woman arrives at a desert trailer, takes the spare key from under a ceramic frog, and finds the cabinets full of Jell-O packages and the fridge full of Jell-O plates. "What the fuck, Doug." A human-shaped figure wrapped in black garbage bags sits in a chair. The screen door slams. Doug, his eyes flat black like a shark's, lifts her and kisses her, and gray tendrils pour from his mouth into hers. Cut to credits. Andre closes the session on Kurt wondering whether "that's what happened to the car", "and then we got to the closing credits." (Walkers 06)

docs.title: Continuity
docs.text:

The double appears in person at the gym in Walkers 07; from the end of that scene Rita secretly plays a replica, and the real Andrew returns in Walkers 09. (Walkers 07, Walkers 09)
  • The note is the bait for the gym meeting in Walkers 07. In that episode Andre tells Rita that the mayor's ring cut in Walkers 05 and the stranger's bite on Huell here were how the skinwalkers took the tissue to copy them; the copy of Huell surfaces in the cold opens of Walkers 07 and Walkers 09. (Walkers 07, Walkers 09)
