docs.title: Crucifixion MO
docs.text:
The Crucifixion MO is the pattern in the first Radford case in which victims were sedated with opiates and Xanax and nailed up, a method the team traces to the three stations in the old church and to a body in the Whateley cellar.

Type Lore / modus operandi Known victims Amanda Lucky; Phoebe Augustine (rescued); Mrs. Whateley; a body in the Whateley cellar later believed to be Abelforth Whateley Site The old-town church; the Whateley house cellar Status Case closed by police on a cartel and serial-killer theory First appearance Radford Horror 05

docs.title: Amanda's autopsy
docs.text:
At the morgue, Dr. Harvey Mauden examines a body believed to be Amanda while the agents watch, and Kurt suggests what to look for. Investigate a Mystery rolls (an 8, then a 10) establish that the nails through her wrists and ankles were pulled through rather than removed, and that lividity shows the blood pooled in her limbs, so she was nailed up. There are no ligature marks, so she was crucified but not otherwise restrained. Her feet are torn up, muddy and cut by brambles. The large wound to her abdomen looks organic, not made by a knife or spear. Dr. Mauden spots old needle scars, at least six or seven months old, and one fresh mark from the last couple of days (Radford Horror 05).

Her toxicology shows trace Xanax and a large quantity of opiates, "enough that she should not have been walking around". Kurt proposes that someone drugged her and she stumbled away because of a pre-existing tolerance, and Mauden says that is what the sheriff's office is thinking too: the other missing people may be held the same way. Mauden also raises the possibility of a spree serial killer who "might be crucifying these women". Dr. Lori's files show Xanax prescribed to Amanda in rising doses with no explanation, but no opiates (Radford Horror 05).

docs.title: The cellar body
docs.text: In Radford Horror 06, in the hidden cellar under the Whateley house, the team finds a dried, long-dead body nailed to rough boards against the wall in an X-shaped pose, its legs spread, with the side of its head stoved in. It appears to have been there for years. Dante remarks that crucifixion on a sideways X is actually the more common form (Radford Horror 06). In Radford Horror 08 the sheriff reports that the body in the hidden basement is probably Abelforth, who "never ran away at all" (Radford Horror 08).

docs.title: The church stations
docs.text: In the abandoned church in Radford Horror 07, a woman hangs crucified on the wall above the pulpit, and the pews have been cleared to make an open space. Two more stations stand beside her, one thoroughly cleaned and the other slick with gore, and medical equipment lies around: syringes, gauze, scalpels and bleach. The woman is breathing; she is Phoebe, alive and unconscious, and Kurt works the nails out with his multi-tool. A pile of dog collars outside ties the place to the missing dogs. The team also finds an open baggie of heroin and syringes. The creature behind the church is the Radford Moth; see Moth life cycle (Radford Horror 07).

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text:
In Radford Horror 08 the sheriff says the police suspect Wilbur was "in bed with the cartel" and sedated his victims with cartel heroin, making him a serial killer. He reports finding the remains of Mrs. Whateley in the back of the church, burned and disemboweled. When the team revisits the burned church, Andre clarifies that she was found crucified. The cascade of gore at the front has been cleaned up and the dog collars removed. Andre confirms that both Amanda and Mrs. Whateley were disemboweled when found (Radford Horror 08).

The players weigh the disembowelments differently. Dante's theory is that Amanda was crucified, escaped through her heroin tolerance and was killed to stop information spreading, while Zack notes that "the Whateley kid who's crucifying people" might also disembowel them. Others suggest the moth ate them (Radford Horror 08). The episodes never state who did the nailing, or whether the sedation came from Dean Lawson's heroin and cash.

docs.title: The Drugged Water
docs.text:
The Drugged Water is the stored water in the Roulet House, which gives the agents hallucinations after they drink it.

Type Lore (hazard) Aliases hallucination water; toilet-tank water Location Roulet House First appearance Roulet Estate 02

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The house has no running water, but the toilet tanks and the water heater still hold some. In Roulet Estate 01, Dante (as Kurt) opens a toilet tank, finds water with some algae growing in it, and drinks it; the others are offered the same, and Kurt drinks more during the day. In Roulet Estate 02 the agents fill bottles from the tanks for their hike (Roulet Estate 01, Roulet Estate 02).

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
• In the basement, Kurt hallucinates veiny hands grabbing his wrists and a Vietnamese prison guard, fires into the trash pit, and comes to curled up on the floor, saying he was "back in Saigon there for a second". He suspects he is "tripping balls" but does not remember taking anything (Roulet Estate 02).
  • Climbing down the chimney, Andrew hallucinates that the bricks turn into muscle that swallows him (Roulet Estate 02).
  • After his hallucination, Andrew realizes that the toilet-tank water tastes weird, and not only from the algae. The water-heater water tastes the same, so the agents stop drinking it. Andrew mimes a warning to the monk, who has a water bottle of his own; Zack voices the monk's reaction to the pantomime as "Ah, perverts" (Roulet Estate 02).
  • In Roulet Estate 03, the agents are still somewhat hungover and feeling "a little bit weird", and Dante (as Kurt) drinks coffee in hopes of flushing the hallucinogens out of his system (Roulet Estate 03).

docs.title: Theories
docs.text: Andrew tells the monk by gesture that the person in the attic was probably drugging the sleeping occupants as well. The green slurry found in the lair is a concentrated peyote preparation, but no one in the episodes connects it to the water, and the drug in the water is never named. It is also never established how the water was dosed, or whether it explains the Roulets' "visitations" (Roulet Estate 02). By the end of Roulet Estate 02 Dante jokes that the agents may simply be "tripping balls off of toilet water" and the "alien" a regular serial killer, even though several of them saw a grey alien (Roulet Estate 02).

docs.title: The dusk event
docs.text:
The dusk event was an electrical and atmospheric anomaly that struck the party's rental van near the gate of the Sherman Ranch at dusk on October 30, 1992, killing every electronic device in the car and sliding the van six inches sideways.

Type Anomalous phenomenon Aliases Electrical anomaly; the event; engine scorch marks Location About 50 feet from the ranch gate, Sherman Ranch Date October 30, 1992, shortly after sunset (5:25 p.m.) Cause Never established First appearance Walkers 03

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The party leaves the ranch in the Plymouth Voyager to start the exhumation paperwork in Ballard and to arrange a night-patrol ride-along. About 50 feet from the gate the van dies, and every electronic device in it goes dead. Howard's pager still works, but the walkie-talkie gives only static (Walkers 03).

Outside the van they hear a high-pitched, tinnitus-like whine. Thin, ominous clouds flicker with lightning, and the hair on their necks stands up. They retreat into the car, which Dante (as Kurt) calls "the Faraday cage." The sky then pulses brighter and dimmer in a stuttering rhythm. Howard photographs it, Kurt and the Biz put in ear protection, and Huell gets a pounding headache. Then the car moves six inches sideways, there is a pop, the engine restarts and the sky stops flickering (Walkers 03).

When Rita (as Howard) says they should not be outside, Dante (as Kurt) answers: "No, your hair's standing up. That's fucking lightning." After the car slides, Dante (as Kurt) chambers a round in his sidearm and says: "Must have been the wind." (Walkers 03)

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
Kurt runs a series of safety checks in the manner of his old unit: he tosses trash out of the window, holds his non-dominant hand out of the door and finds static in the air, and tastes the air, which is normal. Tire trails show that the car was dragged sideways, but there is no sign of what pushed it and nowhere to hide a giant electromagnet (Walkers 03).

The watches record the event unevenly. Kurt's battery watch has stopped, the Biz's cheap digital Casio is permanently scrambled, and Howard's mechanical Fossil still works. Kurt wants to compare the stop time with the readings of Robert Bigelow (Walkers 03).

Under the hood, Kurt finds four or five randomly scattered scorch marks where the metal got hot enough to anneal into a different crystal structure. Howard photographs them and mutters about the 1950s Levelland, Texas case (Walkers 03). Howard raises Levelland again in Walkers 04, after the party finds a crow burned to a crisp that tumbled out of the sky. He tells the deputy driving them that in November 1957 a vehicle broke down near Levelland and a UFO was reported. The case is usually attributed to ball lightning, he adds, although witnesses claimed to see a rocket-shaped object overhead (Walkers 04).

docs.title: Possible connections
docs.text:
Later that evening the party hears loud popping from the substation near the ranch turnoff and sees flickering light. Kurt's Investigate a Mystery roll shows that the equipment is arcing into the ground and being driven far harder than designed, and that something blew into it and created a path to ground (Walkers 03). In the bar, Maggie describes ball lightning that streaked past her car on the ranch's back road and shot straight up (Walkers 03).

The episodes never establish whether the dusk event came from the ranch, the substation, an outside force or something else. It belongs with the other unexplained happenings catalogued under the Sherman Ranch phenomenon. See also the vanishing car and the night event, later anomalies that struck the party's car and house.

  • Walkers 04 (Levelland comparison)

docs.title: Enemy Action
docs.text:
Enemy Action is President George H. W. Bush's explanation for the events in Georgia: that the surveillance of Bill Clinton in the same town as the task force was no accident but a deliberate attack on the continuity of American leadership.

Type Lore (theory) Aliases Bush's theory Held by George H. W. Bush Concerns The Clinton surveillance scandal and the Dahlonega events First appearance Walkers 01

docs.title: The theory
docs.text:
In the Oval Office scene of Walkers 01, Bush tells Andrew Howard that he expects to lose to Clinton within days. He does not believe it was pure coincidence that "some criminal with a bunch of ape-men" was surveilling Clinton in the same town as the task force, and says: "There is coincidence, there is miracle, and there is enemy action. That is enemy action." In his view a power arranged it to remove him from the game and break the continuity of leadership. He says it might be China, the remnants of the Soviets, or "something else altogether, from somewhere else", and adds, "you hit one of them with your car" (Andre (as George H. W. Bush), Walkers 01).

Bush warns that there may be agents working against the country even from within its own organizations. He tells Andrew that whatever the next administration says, he is "personally responsible for the survival of the United States of America". Andrew replies that this has been his responsibility his whole life, then delivers a long talk on the Aetherius Society, the Masters and a "spiritual battery" of good energy, while the camera zooms in on Bush's face going slowly blank (Walkers 01). See Aetherius Society.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
• The scene follows the scandal. Andre later says that since "the double scandal" Ross Perot polls above 45% in most polls, while Bush leads clearly only in Texas (Walkers 01). See Clinton Surveillance Scandal and Alternate history.
  • Bush says he started the task force only because his son, George W., made him promise to look into the paranormal if he won, and that he never believed in "wacky tobacky hootenanny bullshit" and was humoring him (Walkers 01).
  • Bush's tone is grim, but the scene is played for comedy, ending on Andrew's Aetherius Society monologue (Walkers 01).

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
• Whether Bush's "enemy" exists. The ape-man operation in Dahlonega, a gold-mining ring run by Jan Martense, has no clear link to a foreign power. The team does conclude that someone deliberately piped explosive gas into the mines, and the culprit is never identified (see The Crack in the Air). The Biz did receive KGB tasking before the case (see Spy Camera and Microphone), but Bush is never shown learning of it.
  • Who the "enemy agents" inside US organizations might be.

docs.title: Appearances
docs.text: • Walkers 01

docs.title: Exhumation of Shelly Wilmarth
docs.text:
The exhumation of Shelly Wilmarth is the errand that brings the task force to Utah: a client's request to dig up her dead mother's grave in Ballard, which stays pending as the town falls apart around it.

Type Case objective / legal process Aliases Exhumation court order; the exhumation Requested by Alberta Wilmarth Subject Shelly Wilmarth Location Churchyard cemetery, Ballard Status Judge agreed in Walkers 04; dig scheduled but never carried out First appearance Walkers 01

docs.title: The request
docs.text:
In Walkers 01, Alberta Wilmarth knocks on Andrew Howard's door holding a box of documents and tapes and says: "I need you to force the Mormon church to exhume my mom." Her mother, Shelly Wilmarth, died of a heart attack in the winter of 1990, alone with the cattle. Alberta shows an obituary, a yearbook photo, a reunion photo and a VHS copy of local news footage of a community-centre protest in which Shelly appears. The man renting the ranch has also seen her walking the edge of the property at night (Walkers 01).

In the morning Big Bill, stressed, tells Howard that it is the task force's case and the FBI will pay for the plane tickets. Howard announces, "Who wants to exhume a dead woman?" Kurt has a shovel, which Huell had been using on a previous case (Walkers 01). In Walkers 02, as the team leaves the ranch, Alberta asks them to see about the exhumation as soon as they can (Walkers 02).

docs.title: Paperwork and the judge
docs.text:
In Walkers 03, the party sets out to start the process. The players debate what an exhumation would prove, with Dante calling it "the opposite of a welfare check": finding a body would point to a fake or doppelganger, while an empty coffin would point to reanimation or a faked death.

Sheriff McDermish agrees to file the paperwork the next day. He warns that the town's judge is a cantankerous man with old-fashioned views, and that an exhumation sought in a custody dispute about fifteen years earlier went nowhere. At the churchyard the party finds Shelly's grave under a big black granite slab, undisturbed and cleaned, with some trampled grass from a recent visitor. Kurt notes that they could steal the body if the exhumation is denied (Walkers 03).

In Walkers 04, Howard spends hours on the phone with the sheriff, judges and the FBI. His roll (a 7) fails to move a judge who objects for religious reasons, so Rita (as Howard) calls Big Bill, who talks to the judge for twenty minutes and leaves him shaken. The judge agrees, and the exhumation is set for the day after tomorrow (Walkers 04). Walkers 05 opens with Andre's recap that the court order should go through the day after tomorrow, and Dante credits it to "Rita called dad." Later Kurt tells Alberta that the exhumation is going through (Walkers 05).

docs.title: Ground-penetrating radar
docs.text: Because the dig is delayed, the team brings in ground-penetrating radar. In Walkers 06, a scan over the grave, compared against neighbouring plots, shows something solid in the coffin, with about 85% confidence. Dante explains that the scan was a backup in case the order was not approved, and the party concludes that it is worth digging the next day (Walkers 06).

docs.title: Still pending
docs.text: In Walkers 07, Andre reminds the players that they have the exhumation order for the following morning, the same time Donald McManley is due to arrive (Walkers 07). The recorded episodes never show the grave being opened. It is never established whether Shelly's body is in the coffin, or what Alberta saw on the news footage. For Alberta's account of her mother's apparition on the ranch, see Shelly Wilmarth.

docs.title: The beam
docs.text:
The beam is an invisible, switchable line of heat and magnetic force at the fence of the Sherman Ranch, discovered in Walkers 06, which flings ferrous metal along a long arc toward Roosevelt.

Type Anomalous phenomenon Aliases Ranch heat-and-magnet beam; the line Location The yard fence of the Sherman Ranch Direction An arc pointing back toward town, in line with Roosevelt Cause / operator Never established First appearance Walkers 06

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
At the end of Walkers 06, a rattling noise draws the party outside. The party's car, Betsy, is fine, but at the yard fence a sheet of metal is rattling with a faintly glowing vertical line running through it. Dante (as Kurt) throws a rock at it and it glances off the side.

Zack (as Huell) pokes the glowing part with a long stick. The dry grass starts to smoke, he lights a cigarette from it, and his hand heats up as it nears the line. Kurt tears a second sheet of metal off the fence and holds it over the line; it thrashes, is ripped from his hands and shoots skyward. Huell's Read a Bad Situation roll (an 11) shows dust and grit suspended along a curved invisible line, with clouds stretched along it (Walkers 06).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Appearance. The line is invisible apart from a faint glow. It stands vertical, then curves away on an arc, and dust and grit hang suspended along it (Walkers 06).
  • Heat. It heats and rattles metal near it. The hottest point shifts from red to yellow to white, dry grass smokes, a hand held near the line grows hot on both the palm and the back, and everyone's eyes begin to hurt. Dante (as Kurt) says: "Guys, I think we're being microwaved. I think we need to get out of here." (Walkers 06)
  • Magnetic effect. Ferrous metal is strongly affected. The second sheet shoots away along the arc, and Kurt's broken watch, opened into three pieces and held out to the line, rockets upward at incredible speed. A penny is only slightly deflected; Dante points out that pennies are non-ferrous (Walkers 06).
  • Switchable. As the party backs away, a loud electrical pop sounds and all the suspended dust drops, and the rattling stops. Rita (as Howard) says: "They just turned their thing off." (Walkers 06)

docs.title: Connection to the vanishing car
docs.text: Asked which way the arc ran, Andre says it headed back toward town, and when Dante asks whether it pointed toward Roosevelt, answers: "Yes, they're in a line." Dante (as Kurt) remarks that this might be exactly what happened to the party's car, which was found flattened in Roosevelt (Walkers 06). Earlier in the same episode, the junkyard owner Yusuf Ansari, who had been pressured by the Roosevelt police into confessing to crushing the car, told the party that his crusher does not flatten cars that much, and the party noted that there were no tracks around the wreck for a magnetic lifter. The episode ends on this cliffhanger. See also The vanishing car.

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text: The source, the operator and the purpose of the beam are never established. Howard's remark implies that someone controls it. The beam belongs with the other unexplained happenings under the Sherman Ranch phenomenon. The cavern beneath the ranch is not tied to the beam in any episode.

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text: • Dante summed up the scene at the table as "Magnet stole sheet metal." (Walkers 06)

docs.title: Appearances
docs.text: • Walkers 06

docs.title: LA treatment cover story
docs.text:
The LA treatment cover story is the official excuse for the new disappearances in Radford, Virginia: letters and claims that the missing people have gone to rehab or psychiatric care in Los Angeles, backed by lawyers who threaten anyone who investigates.

Type Lore / cover story Aliases missing people in LA treatment Claimed destination A California rehab "like Narconon"; inpatient psychiatric treatment in Los Angeles Status Never verified; the team treats it as a cover First appearance Radford Horrors 02

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: In Radford Horrors 02 the sheriff, Molly Underhill, tells the team about the disappearances that followed Phoebe Augustine's. After Phoebe went missing, the sheriff's office was told she had gone to a rehab in California, "like Narconon", but could not reach her, and nobody in her family knew of a drug problem. Whenever the office asked around, "really scary lawyers" threatened to sue and sent threatening letters, and something similar happened with several other missing people. Visitors are not allowed at the rehab. The sheriff thinks the whole story is suspicious, "especially since" Phoebe was so closely tied to the earlier disappearances, who were "definitely not in rehab". She gives the team the lawyers' phone number, which the earlier FBI task force had also requested, along with a map and missing posters (Radford Horrors 02).

docs.title: Elizabeth George
docs.text:
At the Douglas Pinball Emporium in Radford Horrors 03, Douglas Douglas explains that his overnight worker Elizabeth George was gone when he opened. He found a letter on her door saying she was in inpatient psychiatric treatment in Los Angeles, which he does not believe. The Flash Gordon machine she was repairing had been left open on the floor, there was a bloodstain in the parking lot, and the hand towels were missing from the employee bathroom. The episode's cold open had shown a woman tased and carried off by a man in a black balaclava (Radford Horrors 03).

Kurt recalls that other missing people were supposedly in LA psychiatric treatment, with lawyers threatening anyone who called. Ezra asks whether this was a feature of the first Radford case, and Andre says it was not. Andre adds that officially only a few people are missing, because the rest are "supposedly in drug or psychiatric treatment" at LA facilities (Radford Horrors 03).

docs.title: Escalation to the FBI
docs.text: In Radford Horrors 04, Webster calls Director Rudy Giuliani and passes on the team's suspicions: gray vans that kidnapped at least one person on camera seem to have arrived when the Safe Environment Fund did, and the missing people all left letters saying they had gone to an addiction therapy center in LA. This seems out of character for them, they could not afford it, and nobody is allowed to see or hear from them. Giuliani already has a man looking into the SEF, asks whether the center is "Narcanon" or "Narconon" (the paperwork spells it with an O), and agrees to put one of his researchers on it (Radford Horrors 04). Compare the Acceptable fact pattern order.

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text: Radford Horrors 02 describes the destination as a California rehab, while Radford Horrors 03 and 04 say Los Angeles.

docs.text:

  • Radford Horrors 03
  • Radford Horrors 04

docs.title: The Land Dispute
docs.text:
The Land Dispute is the year-long campaign of eviction letters and pressure by unnamed "corporate goons" to push the Covenant off its land in Auraria, Georgia.

Type Lore (legal and corporate conflict) Aliases corporate goons Affected The Covenant Place Auraria First appearance Appalachia 04

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: In Appalachia 04, River tells the team that the community has deals in the works to get money "to stave off those corporate goons", including a peach orchard arrangement and sales of preserves, so they can hire a lawyer. The goons "started showing up about a year ago" with paperwork claiming some right to the land, and told the community it would be evicted unless it signed the land over. According to River, Elijah Ray says the claim is bullshit and that the people behind it are agents of Satan (Andre (as River), Appalachia 04). The Covenant also holds Auraria to be the Garden of Eden (see Covenant Beliefs).

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Mother Dahlia Riversand fetches the nasty letters. She cannot give them up, since they are for the lawyer, but the team may copy information from them. The letters name a law firm, Jackson and Lee's, and do not say who the client is. Kurt Larson says he will put out feelers (Appalachia 04).
  • The community is short of money. In Appalachia 02 and Appalachia 04 the team sees a stand selling preserves and quilts and members frantically canning in hot tents. The boiler they want, with a contract for February, was delayed because they were saving for the lawyer (Appalachia 04).
  • The community boils its river water and has used what Dahlia thinks are chlorine tablets for about a year, after earlier intestinal trouble. One man lost two toes to an infected toenail, which she does not link to the water. She says she will find out what is in the water when they have a lawyer (Appalachia 04).
  • River says the bathing river carries "a lot of runoff from the Spud Hut plant" (Appalachia 04).

docs.title: Theories
docs.text: The players suspect a link between Spud Hut runoff, the land push and the Covenant, but the episodes never say who is behind the eviction campaign. Jackson and Lee's names no client. At the end of Appalachia 04, the Biz suggests checking the river for chemicals and taking a closer look at Spud Hut, and the team decides to have dinner there first.

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
• Who the client behind Jackson and Lee's is.
  • What Kurt's feelers turned up. Later episodes do not report back.
  • Whether the water problem is connected to the land push.

docs.title: Appearances
docs.text:
• Appalachia 02
  • Appalachia 04

docs.title: Lemuria
docs.text:
Lemuria is a discredited lost continent from real-world fringe history that, in the Marblehead case, surfaces in the Sons of Adam's modified Bible as a sunken Eden and fills a fringe shelf in Amos Shaw's house.

Type Lore (fringe belief) Aliases None; the Bible never names it Associated with Sons of Adam, Amos Shaw First appearance Summer Service 01

docs.title: The real-world theory
docs.text: Andre explains the background at the table. Lemuria was proposed in the 1800s to explain how lemur skeletons got to Madagascar, before continental drift was understood. Continental drift discredited it, but occultists and hippies kept it alive as a kind of "Indian Atlantis." (Summer Service 01)

docs.title: In the Sons of Adam Bible
docs.text:
While the team waits for a girl to come home so they can interview her, Andrew speed-reads the motel's Sons of Adam Bible with a "sick intensity." Rita rolls an 11, a full success, and asks what sort of creature is involved and what is being concealed. Andre's answers describe a text that is mostly the normal Bible with added material:

  • Jesus travels to a lost landmass between India and Madagascar, which is Lemuria even though the Bible never uses the name.
  • The Garden of Eden was on that land bridge and was taken beneath the waves to protect it.
  • On Judgment Day everyone will physically return to Eden.
  • Angry, noticeably worse-written diatribes against continental drift are mixed in, insisting that "the firmament does not shift."
  • The tone around Revelation is hysterical and millenarian, with Jonestown overtones; Andre says that in an FBI agent's professional opinion "the Kool-Aid is no more than five or six years out."

Andrew recognizes the allusions from his own fringe reading. (Summer Service 01)

Rita (as Andrew Howard)

"I think they might sacrifice people to a sea monster."

Dante's Kurt agrees that this is the vibe he got from the front-desk clerk, and compares the church to a Wicker Man cult. Andrew corrects him: "No, they're not wicker people. They're definitely water people. They're wet. They're wet people." (Summer Service 01)

The same themes of water as origin and Eden under the sea recur in the sermon the team hears that night; see Second coming and eschaton.

docs.title: In Shaw's house
docs.text:
In Summer Service 03, Huell searches the largely untouched bedroom of Shaw's house and rolls a 12 on Investigate a Mystery. He finds a bookshelf of academic biblical texts mixed with fringe material about Lemuria. The closet holds clerical garments like those the preacher wore at the church, with signs that others have been removed, and the nightstand holds a grocery bag with roughly ten pounds of clear crystal spheres. (Summer Service 03)

This ties the preacher personally to the lost-continent material. It is never established who wrote the Bible's added text, or whether the church believes the sunken Eden is a real place beneath Marblehead's waters or only a doctrine.

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text: • Zack and Dante riffed on lemurs ("a continent of lemurs") and on Wicker Man during the Bible scene. (Summer Service 01)

docs.title: Appearances
docs.text:
• Summer Service 01
  • Summer Service 03

docs.title: Livestock mutilations
docs.text:
The livestock mutilations are a string of unexplained animal deaths on the Sherman Ranch in Utah, in which sheep burst apart and cattle are found boiled or split open, which the local FBI office blames on lightning.

Type Anomalous phenomenon Aliases Exploded sheep and mutilated cattle; cattle mutilations; boiled cattle Location Sherman Ranch and about half a mile around it Cause Never established First appearance Walkers 01

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
In Walkers 01, Alberta Wilmarth tells Andrew Howard that her family ranch is "cursed", listing boiled cattle, missing pets, UFO lights and Navy people investigating radiation. She describes one steer with half its head split open from steam pressure and its eyes cooked through (Walkers 01).

In Walkers 02, Carl Gardner of the Salt Lake City field office gives a rundown of the local reports: a former Army Ranger on the ranch who shot at a snooper by the barn, a young woman who saw her dead mother, informal reports of lights and lost time, and cattle mutilation. Gardner admits the cattle were "fucked up" but says it was sometimes lightning, and he puts the lost time down to drinking (Walkers 02).

Ranch hand Walt Murphy calls the property "haunted as hell" and asks whether Alberta told the party about the sheep that "kinda exploded". The cattle, he says, were just dead, but the sheep went "poof, you know, bang." Asked how, Andre (as Walt) replies, "You ever microwaved an egg?" and says the chunks were perhaps corgi-sized. Rita (as Howard) remarks that this is less exploded than "the last thing we saw exploded", and Dante (as Kurt) answers, "A man", a reference to the death at Spud Hut in an earlier arc (Walkers 02).

docs.title: Bigelow's measurements
docs.text: Robert Bigelow's team measures electromagnetic and electrostatic fields, radio waves and thermal and acoustic anomalies, recording everything onto big tape reels. Asked about interesting results, Andre (as Bigelow) answers, "Well, some of the sheep exploded," and adds that there are many unexplained heat signatures and electrical events, all localized to the ranch and about half a mile around it, with nothing unusual in town (Walkers 02). The deaths are therefore grouped with the rest of the Sherman Ranch phenomenon.

docs.title: Theories
docs.text: In Walkers 02, Dante (as Kurt) suggests teenagers with pipe bombs, and Walt agrees that was his first thought; the FBI prefers lightning. No episode settles the cause. The later beam, which heats metal and cooks grass, is the closest the story comes to a mechanism, but nobody links it to the animal deaths on screen.

docs.title: The Marblehead explosion
docs.text:
The Marblehead explosion was a 3 a.m. blast out in the harbor of Marblehead, Massachusetts, that blew out windows, killed fish and sickened locals, and the incident that opens the task force's case in The Summer Service.

Type Event / mystery Aliases The offshore explosion; the blast Location Harbor, Marblehead, Massachusetts Time 3 a.m., spring 1992 (the episodes disagree on how long before the case) Cause Unknown First appearance Radford Horror 08

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The blast came from out in the harbor and moved inland. Windows along the shore were blown out, and when the team walks the beach in Summer Service 01 they see broken panes, recently repaired ones and others taped together as a temporary fix. Afterward the town saw dead fish washing up, odd weather, headaches and bad moods, and a number of locals fell ill. (Summer Service 01)

docs.title: The case file
docs.text: The explosion reaches the task force at the end of the Radford case, when a courier delivers an envelope for Andrew. It holds a case file on eight missing people in Marblehead. About a month earlier, Andre explains, an unexplained explosion had blown out windows and sickened townsfolk. The EPA and the U.S. Geological Survey sent a field team to check whether a seabed natural gas leak had ignited, and after the first couple of days nothing more was heard from them. The local police were unresponsive and suspiciously unhelpful. The file adds that Marblehead is famous for a Loch Ness-style sea monster, a big tentacled worm said to grab people and drag them under. (Radford Horror 08) The team follows the survey team's field notes to the inn; see EPA/USGS survey team.

docs.title: What the team learns
docs.text:
• Eyewitness. The fisherman Briggs blames "the goddamn Russians" for a bombing at three o'clock in the morning about a week and a half earlier. Glass was blown over him, a cut in a sensitive spot became infected, and a doctor in Salem had to drain it. He reports dead fish, weird weather, headaches and bad moods, and says, "Maybe the next one will be more successful." (Summer Service 01)
  • The blast center. Walking the beach, Dante rolls a 12 on Investigate a Mystery and learns that the explosion came from out in the harbor and moved inland. He finds the center of the damage and sees something black bobbing among the dead fish, which proves to be a severed arm in a black turtleneck sleeve and glove. (Summer Service 01)
  • A child victim. The Scott family say their daughter fell ill the day after the blast; see Lena Scott. Her pupils were pinholes and she was trembling, and Dante notes that her symptoms resemble a stimulant overdose. The scientists had told the family it was not natural gas. (Summer Service 01)
  • Poison. Later sessions identify the illness as contact with water carrying a synthetic nerve agent.

docs.title: Theories
docs.text:
Several explanations are voiced and none is confirmed. Briggs suspects a Russian test weapon, and other locals favor either Russians or a gas explosion. Andrew, speaking to locals, suggests a sea monster that someone is feeding, and after the dive he reports an "alien submarine" to a contact. (Summer Service 01, Summer Service 03) At the end of the arc a radio contact tells the team that the "advanced team" of his own group is the dead crew on the sea floor, and that their broad-spectrum agent leaked everywhere when they "got blown up." He does not say that this was the 3 a.m. blast. (Summer Service 06)

A separate crater and glassed rock behind the lighthouse are described in Melted shoreline; the episodes never tie them to the harbor blast.

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text: • The episodes give different intervals for how long ago the blast happened. Radford Horror 08 says "about a month ago," with the survey team missing for about four days, and opens on June 15, 1992. Briggs and the Scotts in Summer Service 01 say about a week and a half, Andre says in Summer Service 03 that the scientists have been missing for nearly two weeks, and the mayor says in Summer Service 04 that the scientists left "just over a week ago."

docs.title: The Masters
docs.text:
The Masters are the benevolent, ascended beings at the center of Andrew Howard's faith, who in his account have guided humanity since the Stone Age and whose number includes Jesus Christ.

Type Lore (belief; possibly beings) Aliases Ascended masters; the "masters"; the next master Followers Andrew Howard, his mother, the Aetherius Society, the circle around Mr. King First appearance Radford Horror 01 (the "next master" speech); Radford Horror 04 (the term "masters")

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Masters are known only through Andrew's belief. As he explains it in Radford Horror 04, they are extraterrestrials who have ascended to a higher plane, "come back and communicate to us to try and help us also become masters in the future and join the glorious space civilization that they live in". There have been masters on Earth for the whole of human existence, he says, guiding development and helping humanity out of the Stone Age, and "Jesus Christ himself was one of the masters". The Biz, a lapsed Catholic, objects that this is blasphemy (Radford Horror 04). In Walkers 01 Andrew lays out the wider doctrine for President Bush: cosmic forces push humanity toward a violent future, and a "spiritual battery" of good energy holds them off (Walkers 01).

No episode confirms that the Masters exist. See also Andrew's Condition and the paranatural.

docs.title: The next master
docs.text: In a flashback in Radford Horror 01, Mr. King, who rarely speaks to Andrew one-on-one, tells him that he serves a higher purpose: "The next master is coming. Maybe next year. Maybe in three or four. But not ten." Whether it is "a triumph or a tragedy" depends on how well his organization opens a path "in the minds of the secular people to accept his truth and his laws", and Andrew's purpose is to help it "stand tall and fight back against the forces of silence that would cover up the influences of the cosmic to protect the petty mundane". King ends: "Jesus and the Buddha were not wholly of this world, and neither are you. Remember that." (Radford Horror 01). See Mr. King. The scene does not use the word "Masters", and the episodes never say whether King's organization is the same body as Andrew's church. Nor do they identify the coming master or say what the "forces of silence" are.

docs.title: The Radford Horror
docs.text:
In Radford Horror 04, standing over the remains of the NSA man, Andrew looks to the sky for a UFO and then explains the Masters to the team (Radford Horror 04). In Radford Horror 07, when a psychic probe grabs at him in the church, Andrew says "It's clearly one of the things that the Masters have warned us about", and later, bleeding: "I got prayers, I got the Masters. We got things for this." During the fight he hears a voice in his head cry "Save me, child! You know the ones who made me—" (Radford Horror 07).

In Radford Horror 08 Andrew shouts "Did you know Jesus is one of the Masters?" as a distraction before firing his church mace. Afterward, in the hospital, he gives a speech to the team that "the Masters are one small part of this whole thing", that "they're just trying to guide us to something else", and that there are other things in the universe, some of them bad. The speech fails (Manipulate Someone, 5) and is followed by a long silence (Radford Horror 08).

docs.title: The Things in Appalachia and later arcs
docs.text: In Appalachia 01 Andrew tells his doctor that he thought "the masters were taking sympathy" when his ritual healing worked (Appalachia 01). In Roulet Estate 02 Rita says Andrew knows a couple of Masters but not "who is or isn't a Master these days" (Roulet Estate 02). See Aetherius Society for the church in the Walkers, Roulet and Radford Horrors arcs.

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
• Whether the Masters are real, and whether the creature's "makers" in Radford Horror 07 have anything to do with them.
  • Who "the next master" is and when he arrives.
  • Whether Mr. King's organization and Andrew's church are the same body.

docs.title: Melted shoreline
docs.text:
The melted shoreline is the stretches of Marblehead's coast, and a crater and wall at the lighthouse, that were fused to volcanic glass by something extremely hot, and the subject that makes the town's chief of police freeze when the task force raises it.

Type Phenomenon / evidence Aliases Volcanic glass; glassy shoreline Location Marblehead coast and the lighthouse Cause Unknown First appearance Summer Service 03

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Behind the lighthouse the team finds that the area beside the viewing platform has been obliterated, leaving a crater that takes out one of the railings. The back of the lighthouse is scorched, with bubbled paint and blackened wood. Looking closely with Investigate a Mystery (Ezra's character the Biz rolls a 14 and asks "what happened here"), the team sees drips of volcanic glass down the back wall, spiky glass filaments on the nails that crumble into micro-shards when touched, and crater rock melted smooth into glass. Andre describes it as if glass had condensed on the building "like water condensing on a cold glass." Inside, every piece of glass in the building is broken. (Summer Service 03)

Dante later tells the town leaders that the team saw other stretches of coast that looked melted, and that they were far too big to be lightning. No recorded scene shows the team seeing these; the sighting presumably dates from the unrecorded Summer Service 02 session. (Summer Service 04)

docs.title: The chief's reaction
docs.text: At the end of Summer Service 04, after the Board of Selectmen meeting, Dante asks about "the parts of the shore turned to volcanic glass." The chief of police, who has glared at the party, goes very still. The mayor says he knows nothing about it and suggests lightning, or kids dynamite fishing. Dante answers that it was much too large for lightning, and says the team saw it from a boat near the lighthouse. The mayor tells "Jimmy," the chief, to look into it, and the chief nods. The session ends there, leaving the players unsure whether the reaction was a sign of a cover-up. (Summer Service 04)

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text: The cause is never given. In Summer Service 03 the team has also learned of a humming, lit vessel under the water, and the glass at the lighthouse suggests something extremely hot, but no episode connects the two. In the finale the angel thing gives off heat that blisters paint and bursts tires, though no episode ties it to the glass. (Summer Service 03, Summer Service 06)

docs.title: Minor lore: The Things in Appalachia
docs.text: Minor lore of The Things in Appalachia: smaller theories, local history, rules of the world and running ideas. Larger threads have their own pages, such as The Bigfoot Hoax, Covenant Beliefs and the Clinton Surveillance Scandal.

docs.title: Civil Forfeiture
docs.text: After finding the gold room, the party justifies taking bars under "civil forfeiture." A reasonable amount (small bars in pockets) is fine; an unreasonable amount costs -1 forward to physical rolls until dropped. Huell and the Biz take unreasonable amounts and clink, Kurt takes a reasonable amount "for my wife and kids," Andrew's satchel holds about six bars, and Sheriff Burke takes some to "figure out the legality later." The team means to return for the rest. See Gold Bars. (Appalachia 09)

docs.title: Feral-pig Theory
docs.text: Eddie Jones of the Circle Chasers argues that Bigfoot is really feral humans, in the manner of feral pigs. He wants the group's footage on local news to "build our brand." Vanessa prefers an undiscovered hominid, Andrew and Sloth a werewolf, and Kurt suspects a hoax. See Eddie Jones. (Appalachia 02)

docs.title: Georgia Gold Rush and Trail of Tears
docs.text: Sheriff Burke resents how Dahlonega sells its gold-rush history to tourists. He recalls that the mines were dug mostly by slaves and that Cherokee land was seized, leading to the Trail of Tears. He says he will "take the Bigfoot stuff over the gold stuff." The phrase "gold in them there hills" is also described as a corruption of a local mint man's speech. See Dahlonega. (Appalachia 01, Appalachia 02)

docs.title: Gold Mining Theory
docs.text: The team's working theory links the dirt in the wrecked Spud Hut truck to the tunnels beneath Dahlonega. At Spud Hut Corporate, a man investigating the company guesses "Gold mining?" when Kurt tells him the truck carried only dirt. The theory is confirmed in the ninth episode, when handler Clive explains that ape-men dig the remaining gold because they do not talk. See Jan's Conspiracy. (Appalachia 08, Appalachia 09)

docs.title: Marblehead Cover Story
docs.text: Three versions of the Marblehead incident exist, as Andre lays out in the recap: the code-word classified report kept with Big Bill, a version for the rest of the government in which a religious cult leaked nerve agent into the sea and then made a failed attack on a nuclear plant, with the worms downplayed, and a different public version. Andre likens the incident to the Oklahoma City bombing in scale. The cover story is also the KGB's leverage over the Biz, who is offered information on the "Massachusetts matter." See KGB. (Appalachia 01)

docs.title: Methanol Fermentation and Torpedo Juice
docs.text: Frotter Comstock lectures the team on methanol: natural yeast working on fruit-skin pectin yields it, which makes the Covenant's peach drink risky, and the thermostat on their old McMurray still has been sticking for about twenty-five years. Kurt contributes "torpedo juice," his claim of a naval ethanol fuel mixed with fruit juice. His parting advice is "Good luck keeping those cultists from going blind." See Frotter Comstock. (Appalachia 02)

docs.title: Navy SEAL Trident Tattoo
docs.text: The dead man in the Chewbacca costume bears a faded anchor tattoo on his bicep and a trident on his calf. Kurt, rolling Sharp at -1, is confident the trident is a Navy SEAL emblem. Combined with his military haircut and the missing tags, it marks him as ex-military, though Kurt thinks a SEAL seems "overqualified" for faking Bigfoot. See Troy Cleaver. (Appalachia 06)

docs.title: Never Touched by Human Hands
docs.text: Spud Hut's potato guarantee is that its potatoes are "never touched by human hands," harvested with a special tool and the subject of a presentation on "the future of hygiene." Charlene repeats it when the Biz inspects the lumpy sacks. Kurt asks to see the tool; it is not shown. Meanwhile the wrecked truck's "Potatoes" bags are filled with dirt. (Appalachia 07, Appalachia 08)

docs.title: Philosopher's Fist OVA Retcon
docs.text: At the top of Appalachia 02, Andre explains that he has retroactively decided the non-canon one-shot, Philosopher's Fist 3.J/2: Unchainable, was an OVA that Huell watched on the Smith Hotel's cable TV while falling asleep. (Appalachia 02)

docs.title: Psychic-spy Programs
docs.text: To test Andrew after his sleepwalk, Kurt holds his face and recites the names of real psychic-spy programs: Gondola Wish, Stargate, Grill Flame, Sun Streak, SCANATE, Project CF and Center Lane. Andrew shows only confusion. When Andrew asks whether he should know them, Kurt answers "Not for another ten years." See Kurt Larson. (Appalachia 03)

docs.title: Ritual Healing and Backlash
docs.text: In Andrew's childhood cult, ritual healing is a higher power acting through the healer, and it carries backlash. Andrew says he has healed only twice before, and both times he got a nosebleed. Dr. Arthur explains the mechanism and tells of his own retracted testicle. In Appalachia 03, Andrew uses Lay on Hands on Kurt and takes the harm as a massive nosebleed. See Dr. Arthur. (Appalachia 01, Appalachia 03)

docs.title: Ruby Ridge and Marblehead
docs.text: Past cult incidents are why Big Bill orders the team to run the Georgia case by the book. McManley relays that, because of Ruby Ridge and "that thing in Marblehead," the cult-linked case demands warrants, paperwork and clean hands. See Big Bill. (Appalachia 03)

docs.title: "Water People"
docs.text: In Appalachia 01, Huell (Zack) says his grandfather called odd locals "the water people" because of something in the water around these parts. At the table the phrase becomes a name for the rowdy Daniel boys. See Minor characters. (Appalachia 01, Appalachia 02)

docs.title: Water and Runoff
docs.text: The Covenant's river water is a problem. Clover says the women get yeast infections every two to six months from bathing in it, blaming runoff from the Spud Hut plant. Mother Dahlia Riversand says the water has been boiled and treated with chlorine tablets for about a year after intestinal trouble, and a member lost two toes to an infected toenail. She wants a lawyer to find out what is in it, and saving for the lawyer delayed the boiler. The Biz proposes testing the river. See The Land Dispute. (Appalachia 04)

docs.title: Minor lore: Philosopher's Fist 3.J/2: Unchainable (non-canon one-shot)
docs.text:
Non-canon

This lore belongs only to Philosopher's Fist 3.J/2: Unchainable, a non-canon one-shot presented as an in-universe anime OVA. Nothing here is part of the main campaign's continuity.

Minor worldbuilding of the one-shot, in alphabetical order.

docs.title: Cantus
docs.text: Derk's place or house of origin, known only from his garbled birth name, "Dirk Half Scion of Cantus," which he himself remembers as "Derk Sauce." Mirabeth suspects "Derk" is a fragment of the real name, and Colonel Sparago grants only that it is a nickname. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Gandekian
docs.text: An alien race. As Derk leaves the Alien Faction, he overhears them say that he looks like a stepped-on Gandekian. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Ki
docs.text: Blastable body energy. At the safety briefing, Colonel Sparago asks the entrants to raise a hand if they can channel the energy of their bodies, also called ki, into concentrated blasts, one of the superhuman categories alongside the enormously strong, psychics, wizards and pure martial artists. Ovain fires white ki fire from his fingers, and Mirabeth, when Derk is unsure whether he can, says "You can definitely do that, dear. It's called a punch." (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: The Doping Scandal
docs.text: During the safety briefing an official announces that the tournament is suspended because one of the judges was found to be on steroids, and the president has ordered an investigation. Mirabeth remarks that the president "was just looking for an excuse." Derk hears the word as "asteroid" and whispers that he has been on it before. The suspension sets off Ovain's breakdown. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Tinder
docs.text: This world's online dating. Sparago's aide says that Ovain's online dating, begun as part of his treatment, has gone badly, and that he has been journaling about killing the president again. Ovain departs announcing that he is "leaving this planet and its Tinder." (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Minor lore: Radford (The Radford Horror and The Radford Horrors)
docs.text: This page lists the minor legends, theories, procedures and background details raised in the two Radford arcs.

docs.title: Anunnaki theory
docs.text: Rutherford, the Pay n' Stay clerk, holds a cosmology in which the Anunnaki are spirits who created the universe to harvest its energy and who punish humanity. They can be glimpsed through peyote, ayahuasca and DMT, and he suggests they may be tormenting victims in a kind of hell. (Radford Horror 04) See Rutherford and DMT pipe.

docs.title: Armory curse
docs.text: The Pay n' Stay clerk tells the team that his father believed Radford was cursed because the local armory made the guncotton for the atom bomb. It is presented only as local legend. (Radford Horror 01) See Radford Arsenal.

docs.title: Art Bell radio
docs.text: The late-night paranormal radio program is playing at the Pay n' Stay desk in Radford Horror 01. In Radford Horror 02 the Biz finds Abe's Circuit City radio tuned to the same station, and Rita (as Howard) concludes that Abe's robbery was probably not about money. (Radford Horror 01, Radford Horror 02) See Abe's radio.

docs.title: Bush Sr. dirty-work theory
docs.text: Andre sets out Webster's likely belief: the earlier task force was George H. W. Bush Sr.'s political dirty-work unit, and the "alien stuff" is a cover. That leaves him puzzled why agents sent to a missing-persons case in Radford keep disappearing. (Radford Horrors 02) See Daniel Webster and George H. W. Bush.

docs.title: Changeling
docs.text: "Changeling" is the name the moth creature uses for Andrew, telling him "you have the understanding" and "you know the ones who made me". Later in the same episode Wilbur tells Andrew "You, of all people, you have to understand", and Andrew answers, "Neither are you." In Radford Horrors 04 Rita recalls that the moth called Andrew a changeling who is capable of understanding. (Radford Horror 07, Radford Horrors 04) See The Radford Moth.

docs.title: Chimpanzees and John Travolta
docs.text: Billy Thornton, the homeless man, complains that he was beaten up by chimpanzees and that John Travolta touched him inappropriately, adding that "they got me with their mind control ray". The players take the chimpanzee part seriously, recalling the earlier "space chimpanzees". (Radford Horrors 02, Radford Horrors 04) See Billy Thornton.

docs.title: Curfew and community meeting
docs.text: Molly announces a curfew starting that night and asks the team to speak at a community meeting at 4:30 p.m. at the church. The sheriff speaks first, then the FBI, then the priest. (Radford Horror 05) See Radford church and Molly Underhill.

docs.title: Forces of silence
docs.text: In a flashback, Mr. King tells Andrew that "the next master is coming" within a few years, and that the organization must open secular minds to "his truth and his laws" against "the forces of silence". The phrase refers to those who would cover up the influence of the cosmic. (Radford Horror 01) See Mr. King's organization and The Masters.

docs.title: Good and bad aliens
docs.text: Andrew spends an hour at the Pay n' Stay debating good and bad aliens with the clerk, each holding a competing theory. (Radford Horror 01) See Rutherford.

docs.title: Koschei the Deathless
docs.text: Yeltsin compares skinwalkers to Koschei the Deathless, the shapeshifting figure of Russian folklore, after the Biz explains that they mimic well but are not strategic, turn erratic and violent when confronted, and the older ones are more convincing than the new. (Radford Horrors 01) See Skinwalkers.

docs.title: Local cryptids
docs.text: When Huell asks the sheriff about oddities, he hears of UFO call-ins, Mothman, and a couple of Bigfoot people every summer. Dick asks about Wendigos, and Zack adds the Fairfax Bunny Man and the Wampus Cat. (Radford Horror 02) See Frank Roosevelt.

docs.title: Los ricos tambien lloran and Russian Roseanne
docs.text: In Moscow the Biz watches Russian-dubbed Los ricos también lloran (The Rich Also Cry) for about three hours with his guard, who sits at a little table crying, eating the borscht the Biz disliked. The soaps are the in-universe television of his captivity. (Radford Horrors 01) See Biz's guards.

docs.title: Marblehead nuclear incident
docs.text: In Radford Horrors 01, the team is reminded that a nuclear weapon was used on the Marblehead sea creature, the angel, in the aftermath of The Summer Service. See Marblehead and The Marblehead explosion. (Radford Horrors 01)

docs.title: Rabies treatment protocol
docs.text: Rabies treatment is immunoglobulin first, then weekly vaccines; the DFA test on the rat is run in Roanoke, and Andrew is told to expect a four-vaccine series if the rat tests positive. Andrew reacts badly to the shots. (Radford Horrors 02, Radford Horrors 03) See Rabid mouse and Field medical kit.

docs.title: Radford old town flood
docs.text: The old town is a colonial settlement that was flooded and abandoned. Its stone church survived the flood but burned during the fight with the moth. (Radford Horror 08) See Radford old town and mill.

docs.title: Reported UFOs and night lights
docs.text: Locals call the sheriff about UFOs and lights in the woods, while light aircraft out of Roanoke Airport fly at night. (Radford Horror 02) See Roanoke Airport.

docs.title: Right to roam controversy
docs.text: The diner waitress says gray vans began appearing a couple of months earlier around the "right to roam" fuss about the woods, possibly tied to the Safe Environment Fund and its fences. (Radford Horrors 04) See Safe Environment Fund and Gray van crew.

docs.title: Tulpa
docs.text: Kurt mentions "the Tulpa thing" as the one past job in which weird spiritual work may have worked, while tripping on the drive back. In Radford Horrors 03 the idea returns as his theory for Andrew's dream dad. (Radford Horror 03, Radford Horrors 03) See Andrew's alien dad.

docs.title: Welding-glass protection
docs.text: Even through a welding mask, the flashlight weapon's beam is blinding and leaves spots in the user's vision when Kurt tests it. (Radford Horror 08) See Flashlight weapon and Tinfoil welding mask.

docs.title: Wilbur-creature psychic link
docs.text: Wilbur feels the creature's pain as physical agony without wounds, and his shoulders dislocate as he thrashes. Rita worries that killing the creature might harm him. (Radford Horror 07) See Wilbur Whateley.

docs.title: Minor lore: The Roulet Estate
docs.text: Minor lore entries of The Roulet Estate, in alphabetical order. Larger topics of the arc have their own pages, including Andrew's Condition, The Drugged Water and Chimney Passages.

docs.title: Christmas Eve Secret Santa
docs.text: The "twenty-five days ago" flashback in Roulet Estate 01, set at the task force office on Christmas Eve 1992 after fifty-three days of paperwork on Utah. Diane gives watercolor paper for Kurt's daughter, a hand-knit sweater for Andrew, scotch for Huell and new shoes for the Biz. Diane receives Andrew's pashmina shawl, Kurt's stolen NSA chair, Huell's scotch and the Biz's Southwestern scratch-off tickets, some already scratched. Among the agents, Kurt gives Andrew a fake alien fetus in a jar, Andrew gives Huell a Dunhill lighter and cigar cutter, Huell gives the Biz a fake ID and the Biz gives Kurt a floppy disk. The exchange is interrupted by Big Bill, who eats biscochitos and gingerbread and brings news that the task force will be disbanded. Andre noted at the table that the time skip had skipped over Christmas, which is why the party is staged as a flashback. (Roulet Estate 01)

docs.title: David Huggins Paintings
docs.text: Paintings by the real-world artist David Huggins, who painted his claimed experiences with a gray alien girlfriend. Zack showed them at the table as the visual reference for the intruder: naked, unnaturally thin and long-limbed, with a classic grey face. (Roulet Estate 01) See also The Roulet Intruder.

docs.title: February 1993 WTC Bombing
docs.text: The real-world bombing of the World Trade Center, which becomes Andrew Howard's desk case in New York in the epilogue. He analyzes bomb photographs from an office high enough up to be unaffected by the blast, making notes for the FBI on the types of bombs used and their consequences. (Roulet Estate 03) See also World Trade Center.

docs.title: Inauguration Day 1993
docs.text: The title card of the cold open in Roulet Estate 01, and the day on which the four agents wake up sick in the abandoned Rhode Island living room. It is also the day on which Ross Perot is to disband the task force. In Roulet Estate 02 Big Bill is said to be due to be fired "sometime today." The flashbacks are labelled "78 days ago" and "Twenty-five days ago." (Roulet Estate 01, Roulet Estate 02) See also Perot's Insurgency Task Force.

docs.title: Jonestown Cover Story
docs.text: Big Bill's official explanation for the Utah disaster. In Roulet Estate 01 the table settles on a radical domestic insurgency: a cult compound under the multimillion-dollar community center, embezzlement to fund a violent uprising, and a Jonestown-style mass killing when investigators arrived. The agents listen in bed to radio reports of the incident and of Perot's victory. Andre puts the deaths at roughly three or four hundred across the two towns. (Roulet Estate 01)

docs.title: Kurt's Portal Theory
docs.text: Kurt Larson's private belief, voiced in the April 1993 epilogue, that a force "on the other end of a portal" is covertly influencing America. His discreet feelers turn up nothing credible or verifiable, nobody takes him seriously, and he usually stops pressing before people tap out. (Roulet Estate 03)

docs.title: Lost Time
docs.text: Missing time, a classic sign of abduction. Kurt Larson loses a minute while hammering at the steel door of the weapons closet, just after Andrew Howard glimpses a brilliant light streaking through the woods. The others find him staring at the door, dizzy and disoriented. The Roulets' own notebook also records lost time. (Roulet Estate 01) See also The Roulets' Notebook.

docs.title: Roseanne
docs.text: The TV show that signals rock bottom. In March 1993 Huell Kendrick day-drinks and watches it, something he had earlier told McManley was rock bottom. By the end of the epilogue Kurt and Andrew are watching it too, Kurt in his hotel and Andrew in New York. It returns in Radford Horrors 01. (Roulet Estate 03)

docs.title: Minor lore: The Summer Service
docs.text: These are the smaller pieces of worldbuilding, period detail and procedure that surface during the Marblehead case. Larger topics have their own pages, such as the glow, Lemuria and the synthetic nerve agent.

docs.title: Crystal Pepsi
docs.text: A period brand that anchors the case in the spring and summer of 1992. Andre pauses to check when Crystal Pepsi came out, then confirms it was April 13th and that it had "just come out." Andrew spits the church's communion wine into an empty Crystal Pepsi bottle outside the service, and the bottle carries the sample to McManley for analysis. See Communion wine. (Summer Service 03)

docs.title: FBI 48-hour hold rule
docs.text: An arrest procedure that comes up in Summer Service 04, after Dante has floated kidnapping the mayor. Ezra asks whether the team can hold people without pressing charges for 48 hours, and Andre answers that the agents have 48 hours to deliver a suspect into custody and have them formally charged, during which time the suspect must be given basic rights, though not necessarily held at an FBI facility. See Mayor of Marblehead. (Summer Service 04)

docs.title: FBI cover-up of strange cases
docs.text: In Summer Service 05 Andrew tries to reassure Madeline Weathers that the Bureau has dealt with cases like hers before. He asks whether she has ever read about "Bigfoot fighting Mothman alien stuff" and believed it, and says the public never hears of such cases because "we don't need everybody knowing how weird the world gets." See Paranatural Incident Task Force and Acceptable fact pattern. (Summer Service 05)

docs.title: Jesus as alien
docs.text: Andrew's stated belief. When Madeline Weathers demands his "position on Jesus Christ," he answers that Jesus was an all-powerful alien who came to Earth to help humanity and guide it to a better future. The Biz says he wasn't sure he believed in God six months ago, but is starting to come around to the idea. See also The Masters and Aetherius Society. (Summer Service 05)

docs.title: SKYHOOK
docs.text: The code word under which the task force's reports are classified. Andre explains the chain above the team: Andrew reports to Big Bill Nelson, head of the Foreign Influence Task Force, since alien visitations are "foreign by definition." Nelson reports to Deputy Director Floyd Clark, and Clark reports to President George H. W. Bush. See Foreign Influence Task Force and Big Bill. (Summer Service 03)

docs.title: Minor lore: The Walkers in Skin
docs.text: This page lists the smaller theories, local customs, historical references and in-world details of The Walkers in Skin; the arc's larger mysteries include Replication, the portal and Disappearances in Ballard.

docs.title: Ballard school smell
docs.text: An eye-watering stench in the Ballard high school, which Harrison describes in Walkers 04 as a problem "this semester." Students guess a sewer or a dead thing in the air conditioning, and Kurt links it to the odd-tasting water. By Walkers 08, when the team recalls the missing schoolchildren, the smell is understood as a clue to the bodies stored at the school. See Ballard High School and plastic-wrapped bodies. (Walkers 04, Walkers 08)

docs.title: Doppelganger theory
docs.text: Andrew's first explanation for Shelly Wilmarth being seen alive. He rules out a secret twin, since Shelly had only brothers, and says doppelgangers copy children, but when he hears that she died alone he puts the idea "back on the list" and delivers an infodump. (Walkers 01, Walkers 03)

docs.title: Early 90s radio
docs.text: Songs that the car radio plays during the drives of Walkers 07: "Baby Got Back" and "Under the Bridge" on the way into Ballard, "Smells Like Teen Spirit" while Huell waits in the car, and "I'm Too Sexy" as he races to the burning gym. "Bohemian Rhapsody" is also heard charting. See the show. (Walkers 07)

docs.title: Friend of Bonaparte
docs.text: A passphrase that Gardner gives the team for a 20 percent FBI discount on gas at a gas station near the Salt Lake City office: they are to say they are "a friend of Bonaparte." (Walkers 02)

docs.title: Funeral potatoes
docs.text: A Utah casserole of cheesy potatoes with a cornflake topping, recommended by Gardner along with dirty soda, Jell-O salad and Frog Eye Salad. The beehive clerk explains that the dish is brought to funerals because it is easy and tasty, and the Good Hills Diner serves it. Huell's stomach turns at yet another potato-based investigation. (Walkers 02, Walkers 04)

docs.title: Howard's angels and ghosts view
docs.text: Andrew's position that ghosts are not real, because they lack physical bodies, while angels are real but poorly understood physical beings. He says the "astral body" is really a form of telepathy. The view colors the anonymous note, which tells him "you have angels" (see the anonymous note). It echoes his catchphrase "ghosts aren't real." (Walkers 06)

docs.title: Levelland case
docs.text: A 1957 vehicle-stalling UFO case from Levelland, Texas, which Andrew cites after the dusk event, where the scorch marks in the engine recall it. He raises it again over the burned crow. He notes that witnesses at Levelland saw a vehicle rather than lights. See the dusk event. (Walkers 03, Walkers 04)

docs.title: Neurological disruption warfare
docs.text: Kurt's CIA-flavored cover explanation for the night event, based on his claimed training against Russian neurological-warfare techniques such as low-voltage current, magnets and novel hallucinogens. He offers it to Bigelow, while Andrew thinks the event was a near-abduction. See the night event. (Walkers 05)

docs.title: Protocol blue
docs.text: Bigelow's lockdown order, which he declares when Kurt reports the missing students and the sheriff's departure: he unlocks "the big cabinet," hands out SPAS-12s and M16s, and sets a ground-floor defensive perimeter. He asks the party to stay as backup. See Bigelow's research operation. (Walkers 07)

docs.title: Pueblo ruins
docs.text: Ruins bulldozed to make way for the Ballard community center. Locals protested, the protest was covered by state news, and graffiti accuses the builders of cultural genocide. The coverage of this protest is where Alberta saw her dead mother. See the community center. (Walkers 03)

docs.title: Skinwalker Ranch basis
docs.text: The arc's real-world model. The setting is an open pastiche of Skinwalker Ranch in Utah. In Walkers 02 Zack asks whether they are going to "the literal Skinwalker Ranch," and Andre answers that they are going to Sherman Ranch. In Walkers 06 Andre explains that it is set before the real ranch was renamed, so it is "only Sherman Ranch at this point in history." When the table looks up the area, Ezra notes a UFO Valley campground next to the real ranch. See Sherman Ranch. (Walkers 02, Walkers 06)

docs.title: X marks
docs.text: Sharpie Xs that the party draws on themselves in Walkers 09 to tell friend from copy. The skinwalker duplicate of Andrew bears one too, and Huell acts on that, knowing that one of the two Howards is a fake. Kurt marks his brow before the infiltration of the cavern. (Walkers 09)

docs.title: Radford's missing dogs
docs.text:
Radford's missing dogs are a long-running pattern in Radford, Virginia, in which large dogs vanish from houses bordering the national forest, an unexplained phenomenon that the team eventually ties to the Radford Moth.

Type Lore / phenomenon Aliases dog-taker; dog collars Location Radford, Virginia, houses backing onto the Jefferson National Forest Explanation Fed to the moth First appearance Radford Horror 01

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
On the team's first evening, as they walk to a payphone, Kurt passes about forty missing-dog posters on the telephone poles, mostly for different dogs (Radford Horror 01). In Radford Horror 02 Andrew searches the sheriff's records and finds a thick folder of complaints going back a couple of years and ramping up over the last six to eight months. The sheriff's notes in the folder read "Why so many dogs? Perverts???", underlined repeatedly. Andrew notices that no dog under about 40 pounds has been taken. An old woman on Berkeley Street keeps complaining that the police are not taking the loss of her Doberman, Harvey Milk, seriously. No remains of any missing dog have been found, though some of the dogs do turn up as ordinary runaways. Huell marks each disappearance on a Pay n' Stay tourist map with a Sharpie, and (on an 8) finds that every house borders the woods (Radford Horror 02).

Dr. Lori tells the team that Abe took the loss of the family dog "pretty hard" before he ran away (Radford Horror 02). See Radio Shack spacesuit robbery.

docs.title: Theories
docs.text: Sheriff Frank Roosevelt favors perverts, given the size of the dogs. The team's own theories include bears, coyotes, wolves, mountain cats, dog fighting, and a wild man in the woods; Ezra's own hypothesis is that Abe, contacted by aliens, is living in the forest and eating dogs. Dante argues that a population of perverts big enough to take that many dogs would show up in other ways. The team discusses staking out the woods with a dog as bait, and Kurt warns that any moving parts around the animal would ruin the plan (Radford Horror 02). In Radford Horror 04, Rutherford, the Pay n' Stay clerk, offers his own view: whatever is taking the dogs and the people may be sending them to some kind of infinite torment (Radford Horror 04).

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Radford Horror 03 opens on a cold open in the woods: a pile of dog collars, footsteps, and another collar thrown onto the pile before the credits (Radford Horror 03).
  • In Radford Horror 04 the Biz tracks the craft along the treeline behind suburban houses, sees it dip into a backyard, and finds a doghouse with a snapped leash and no dog. He reports this to Andrew, who calls it "dog abductions" (Radford Horror 04).
  • In Radford Horror 05 the team finds the skull and part of the spine of a poodle-like dog, about a week old, a quarter mile from the Lucky house, the bones cracked open and the flesh gouged away. Kurt takes the skull as a sample (Radford Horror 05).
  • In Radford Horror 07 a pile of dog collars sits outside the old-town church, alongside a new padlock on the doors (Radford Horror 07).
  • In Radford Horror 08 the pile of collars has been removed from the church, along with the gore and the moth itself, which Ezra's Investigate a Mystery roll (a 9) reads as evidence being concealed, and the team suspects the cleanup crew. Dante sums up the case as a moth monster that influenced a boy to kill for it and "was eating dogs". Wilbur's journal records that the larva loved beef (Radford Horror 08).

docs.title: Moby-Dick book cipher
docs.text:
The Moby-Dick book cipher is the code system, keyed to a 1980 reprint of Moby-Dick, through which the Biz's Russian correspondents send him numbered messages by recorded "sweepstakes" phone lines.

Type Lore (communication method) Aliases Torn-out Moby-Dick; the Moby Dick codebook; the sweepstakes numbers Used by Dick "The Biz" Baxter Senders The "Russian intelligence service" (Summer Service 04); a KGB front (Appalachia 01) First appearance Summer Service 04

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: A recorded voice on a payphone line advertises a "promotional sweepstakes" and reads out lists of numbers ("our winning numbers are 178, 14, 97, 325..."), signing off "Best of luck! Everyone's a winner!" The Biz decodes them against a specific edition of Moby-Dick. A word that does not appear in the novel cannot be sent as written, which is why "Georgia" arrives as "George I A" (Summer Service 04, Appalachia 01). Decoding the first message takes the Biz about ten minutes of laborious work.

docs.title: The Summer Service
docs.text: In Summer Service 04 the Biz's secret instructions require the big 1980 reprint of Moby-Dick, which he does not carry. He jogs to the Readful Things bookstore in Marblehead, using the hotel's lack of toilet paper as his excuse, and finds the right edition (Summer Service 04). About four hours later he sends the others away and phones the number from a payphone. Andre has him decode a message "from the Russian intelligence service": "Two secret[?] submarine lost near Massachusetts. Cause unknown. Instructions to follow soon." The Biz concludes that the Russians probably were not behind the Marblehead events, since, in Ezra's words, "They also lost submarines", and keeps the message to himself (Summer Service 04). The word "secret" is hard to make out in the recording.

docs.title: The Things in Appalachia
docs.text: The cipher returns in Appalachia 01. The Biz gets a sweepstakes invitation that Andre calls a KGB front and rings the "Canada maple syrup sweepstakes line". The numbers (13, 45, 196 and so on) decode to an offer: information on the "Massachusetts matter" in exchange for a favor (Appalachia 01). See KGB.

docs.title: The Radford Horrors
docs.text: When the Biz disappears, the team searches his apartment and finds a copy of Moby-Dick with its first few hundred pages removed. Some of the pages lie in the wastebasket with words circled and underlined, and a chart of numbers and arrows is in the back. The circled words read "instructions to cause soon submarine lost near", though the team cannot tell their order and can see the set is incomplete. All seven words occur in the Summer Service 04 message ("Two secret[?] submarine lost near Massachusetts. Cause unknown. Instructions to follow soon."), although nobody at the table makes the connection. Rita, as Andrew, briefs Kurt that the Biz is "weirdly into sweepstakes" and "receiving coded messages through the book Moby-Dick", and hands over the book and the crumpled pages (Radford Horrors 01). The same apartment holds months of unopened mail and a bug-out bag.

docs.title: Unresolved
docs.text:
• Andre presents both the Summer Service 04 messages ("Russian intelligence service") and the Appalachia 01 messages ("KGB front") as coming from the same Russian source, but the two arcs use differently named sweepstakes lines.
  • The "instructions to follow soon" are never shown to arrive, and it is not established whether the torn copy in the Biz's apartment is the book he bought in Marblehead.

docs.title: Moth life cycle
docs.text:
The moth life cycle is what the team pieces together, mostly from Wilbur Whateley, about how the Radford Moth grew from an oversized caterpillar into a telepathic creature that is born pregnant and uses women as hosts, like a parasitic wasp.

Type Lore / biology Aliases moth hosting; egg count; Morpho menelaus Subject The Radford Moth Sources Wilbur Whateley; Wilbur's journal First appearance Radford Horror 07

docs.title: Born pregnant
docs.text: In the old church, with a gun to his head, Wilbur tells the team: "I've been with it for so long, and it's more sentient than we are. It's not wrong if it kills us. Like, it's not wrong when you eat a chicken. And it has to breed. They're born pregnant." Once he is cuffed, he turns to Andrew and says, "You, of all people, you have to understand" (Radford Horror 07).

docs.title: Larva to moth
docs.text: Wilbur's journal in Radford Horror 08 gives the timeline: he found a larva resembling Morpho menelaus, but much larger and abnormal, on June 3rd, fed it beef, and wrote that "she hatched hungry" on August 15th. He began to hear a voice that he could barely tell from his own ("She's talking all the time now"), and he adored it ("She's so beautiful ... she's mine"). The journal does not give a year. The creature is a huge moth with a proboscis and razor claws, raised first in the Whateley basement and then moved to the old church (Radford Horror 08).

docs.title: Hosting
docs.text:
In Radford Horrors 04 the team questions Wilbur at the Roanoke mental hospital. He recognizes them "from the church", says he dreamed of "drowning in blue", that something was "wearing" him, and that he found a Morpho menelaus caterpillar in the woods that was somehow wrong. After Kurt's partial success on a Manipulate Someone roll, Wilbur says it felt "like the ocean ... like a mother", in the basement: "It was pregnant. It needed to breathe. It need--oh god, it needed hosts, like a parasitic wasp. Those women--". As the staff escort them out he adds, "I found it under a white oak." (Radford Horrors 04)

Later in the episode Andrew asks the others how many young a moth has at a time. Kurt rolls a 10 on Sharp, and Andre, saying he saw it on the Discovery Channel, tells the table the answer is between 40 and 500 eggs (Radford Horrors 04).

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text: Wilbur's line "It needed to breathe" is probably "it needed to breed", given what he says in Radford Horror 07. In Radford Horror 08, Kira jokes about "no possibility of there being eggs anywhere" after the church fire, and the moth's body is gone when the team returns. Whether any eggs survived is never answered in the episodes, although Kurt's working theory in Radford Horrors 04 is that the Emporium intruder was a juvenile moth or a thrall; the episodes do not confirm it.
