docs.title: The night event
docs.text:
The night event was a nocturnal anomaly over the party's guest house on the Sherman Ranch, in which each agent suffered a different hallucination, Andrew Howard levitated, the Biz lost every dental filling, and the house shifted on its foundations before a flood of white light ended it.

Type Anomalous event Aliases Psychic modulation event (Kurt's term) Location The guest house ("little house") on the Sherman Ranch Date The night before Election Day, early November 1992 Cause Never established First appearance Walkers 05

docs.title: The event
docs.text:
After a cold afternoon spent chaining their car to four posts in front of the big house, the party goes to bed in the guest house. In Walkers 05, each of them is hit by a separate hallucination:

  • Huell wakes to screaming as the world pivots 90 degrees and the house feels like a tumble dryer. He goes to look for the source, gun in hand. His Act Under Pressure roll (a 6, with a minus one) fails, and he crashes through the little card table next to the fridge.
  • Kurt wakes in Saigon, with jungle, wild pigs scampering through the undergrowth and a pounding head. He shouts in Vietnamese, "You'll never take me alive," and takes cover behind the dresser, which is the nearest bush. His roll to remember his mission is a mixed result: part of him still believes he is in Saigon, so he bites his LSD tooth to shift into a more familiar broken state.
  • The Biz wakes to find the left side of his visual field is outer space, crumbling away down the middle, with a horrible keening noise. His hands shake uncontrollably and he tastes blood.
  • Andrew Howard believes he has been buried alive, freezing and hammering on the edges of his coffin.

Kurt sees the refrigerator, which is screaming, as the trunk of an ancient tree and opens it. Andrew spills out, flailing, and begins to float toward the ceiling; Kurt pulls him down by the ankle toward a bed as white light pours through the windows. Everyone drops to the carpet, and their cognition returns to normal apart from the effects of Kurt's LSD tooth. Andrew lands badly on his shoulder but takes no harm because of the pendant he never takes off, and Rita (as Andrew) is furious that he "almost got abducted" (Walkers 05).

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text:
• The Biz's teeth. He finds in the mirror that every one of his fillings is gone. Kurt, citing his training for a "psychic modulation event", has him swish cocaine from the heel of Kurt's shoe around his mouth, which stops the bleeding. The next morning Walt drives the party to a Roosevelt dentist, who has never seen someone lose all his fillings and has only gold to replace them with; Dante (as Kurt) notes that gold is non-magnetic (Walkers 05).
  • The house. Guns, badges and wallets are scattered, the silverware is in a pile on the couch, and the phone is on the other side of the room. Outside, the house has shifted a few inches, so that the stairs no longer line up with the front porch, and it feels noticeably warmer than the surrounding air (Walkers 05).
  • Bigelow's response. Robert Bigelow phones asking whether they saw a light; a white floodlight woke him. Later he shows the party a frozen frame from the sky camera and asks whether they have heard of the Black Sun. The thermal camera whited out. He agrees to set up a big ring of cameras around the party's house, and says that his staff have had nightmares and been prescribed sleep aids (Walkers 05).
  • Video. The footage shows a bright white ring with a slightly purple glow, oscillating for seconds. Bigelow calls it a clear-cut event that has been escalating nonlinearly for a few weeks, and says the team "may be on the verge of making contact" (Walkers 05).

docs.title: Theories
docs.text: Kurt tells Bigelow that the agency trained him for the possibility that the Russians would develop some kind of neurological weapon. Andrew thinks the party narrowly missed being abducted (Walkers 05). The party gives Bigelow's staff psychiatrist a 45-minute debrief, in which the Biz holds back the fillings and shares the neurological disruption. It belongs with the other happenings in the Sherman Ranch phenomenon, alongside the dusk event and the vanishing car.

docs.title: Memorable quotes
docs.text:
Quote

"God damn it, I almost got abducted. Why weren't the windows open?" Rita (as Andrew Howard), after the event.

docs.title: The 1992 OVA Framing
docs.text:
Non-canon

The OVA framing belongs to the non-canon one-shot Philosopher's Fist 3.J/2: Unchainable, not to the main campaign.

The 1992 OVA framing is the conceit that Philosopher's Fist 3.J/2: Unchainable is an anime original video animation, a show within the show, that Huell Kendrick watched on hotel cable TV during The Things in Appalachia.

Type Lore (framing device) Aliases Show-within-a-show; the 3.J/2 title First appearance Philosopher's Fist

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The one-shot was recorded as a separate session, with no agents of the task force in it. In the Appalachia recap, Andre explains that the team stays at the Smith Hotel, "which is actually pretty nice, and has cable TV," and that he decided, retroactively, "that the stupid fucking shonen arc we did was an OVA that Huell watched on the hotel's cable TV as he was falling asleep." (Appalachia 02)

Within the main campaign's 1992 setting (see The show), the one-shot is therefore an early-1990s anime that happens to be playing on a hotel television. The session itself never mentions the task force, the FBI or the year. It has no cold open, "previously on" or credits, and the player characters are not any of the campaign's agents. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: The title joke
docs.text: Partway through the session, as Derk is talking to the president, Andre says, "Also, I forgot to mention it, but this is the title of the anime that we are in." Dante replies, "Three Point J over Two," which gives the show its name, Philosopher's Fist 3.J/2: Unchainable. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Dub voices
docs.text: At the start of the session, Andre asks Rita to do a "dub voice," as in an anime English dub. She says she has "only got the one old person voice," so Mirabeth keeps it. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: OVA conventions in play
docs.text:
The session plays with the conventions of tournament anime:

  • the tournament arc, with a grand prize, judges and a doping-scandal plot trigger
  • ki blasts, which Andre calls "pew-pews," and white fire
  • a rival with a tragic past, Ovain, and a training mentor, Mirabeth
  • an alien prince, Derk, whose name is a garbled fragment of a longer one
  • over-the-top jumps into space
  • the rival's salute and farewell ("I salute you... I'm going back home"), and the mentor's parting promise to meet "next year at the tournament"
  • a cliffhanger ending, with Derk stranded in Wisukonshin

Matt compares Derk's backstory to Hunter x Hunter, and the rules the table uses are described on Game System. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text: • Mirabeth and Derk already have established protocols (jumping straight up as a signal, "follow the arrows"), suggesting a history before the session that is never shown.

docs.title: Appearances
docs.text: • Philosopher's Fist

docs.title: The Flag Contest
docs.text:
Non-canon

The Flag Contest belongs to the non-canon one-shot Philosopher's Fist 3.J/2: Unchainable, not to the main campaign.

The Flag Contest is the national-holiday event at which children from disadvantaged communities show the president their designs for the tournament's logo, and the way Mirabeth schemes to get the over-age Derk into the president's presence.

Type Lore (event) Aliases Children's logo-flag event; the pre-event social Location Community center, then the Presidential Event Hall First appearance Philosopher's Fist

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: After the safety briefing, Mirabeth asks whether the president's office has any child-outreach event she can sneak Derk into for publicity. Her Assess the Situation roll (a 9, with a -1 because there might not be one) reveals that a national holiday is associated with the tournament, on which kids from disadvantaged communities show off the promotional art they made for the logo. One design is picked, and a professional graphic artist turns it into the real logo. An old bridge buddy of Mirabeth's is on the committee. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: The scheme
docs.text:
On a video phone Mirabeth calls her friend, claiming Derk is 14. The age limit for the event is 15. Her Pierce the Mask roll fails (3), so she gets only a place on the wait list and the address of a pre-event social in the Capital. The friend is briefly confused when Mirabeth asks about peers for Derk, since the tournament's own entry limit is 17. (Philosopher's Fist)

Mirabeth sends Derk to the Public Library to draw a flag, and then tears the result off the floor. At the community-center social, ten blocks away, the other children are at-risk teens. A bully insults Derk, and he does not understand it; a kind 14-year-old, Sarah, then befriends him and shows him her flag. Mirabeth meets Addison and her son and sells the oil pyramid. That night the friend calls to say a spot has opened up for Derk, who does not draw a better flag and keeps the stars and scorpions. The next morning, in a line of disadvantaged youths, he presents his flag to the werewolf president. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text: • Matt made flags for an in-joke "flag contest" on the table's Discord; Andre noted that he had not yet seen them.

docs.text: • Philosopher's Fist

docs.title: Game System
docs.text:
Non-canon

This game system belongs to the non-canon one-shot Philosopher's Fist 3.J/2: Unchainable, not to the main campaign.

The Game System of Philosopher's Fist 3.J/2: Unchainable is a Powered by the Apocalypse game whose stats, conditions and playbooks follow the superhero game Masks, in contrast to the Monster of the Week rules of the main campaign (see Game mechanics).

Type Lore (rules) Aliases Powered by the Apocalypse; Masks-style GM Andre First appearance Philosopher's Fist

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Andre says the game is Powered by the Apocalypse "but it's a little bit different," calls its rules document "really wordy," and looks up rules live during play. He and Rita check the text together for moves such as Defend Someone. Dante keeps his character sheet in a drawing program, so he is unsure how harm is tracked and writes down one harm for now. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Stats
docs.text: Danger, Freak, Savior, Superior and Mundane. Andre describes Mundane as "human interpersonal charisma." (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text: Afraid, Angry, Guilty, Insecure and Hopeless. Mirabeth marks Insecure after failing to slap Mr. Cartwright. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Moves
docs.text: Assess the Situation, Defend Someone, Directly Engage a Threat, Provoke Someone, Pierce the Mask and Unleash Your Powers.

docs.title: Playbooks
docs.text:
The Bull (Derk, played by Dante). Dante introduces the ability with "as the Bull... as defender, roll Danger instead of Savior." Derk rolls Danger in place of Savior when defending, and Danger in place of Freak for Unleash Your Powers, which Dante calls "physics." He also has a base -1 to Superior.

The Legacy (Mirabeth, played by Rita). Rita refers to one of her moves as "a Legacy one." Mirabeth's abilities include godlike beauty, legendary speed, Symbol of Authority (give an NPC an order based on an authority they recognize; on a hit they choose to do what she says, get out of her way, attack at disadvantage or freeze) and Divine Armor (force-field bubbles of limited range). Her Danger is -1.

docs.title: Notable rolls
docs.text:
• Derk's Defend on Ovain's blast: 5 + 2 = 7, a minimum success. He escalates, and the blast backscatters into Ovain's eyes.
  • Derk's wall jump: Danger 8, costing 1 harm (a twisted ankle). Mirabeth rolls Danger to hold on: 12 with her -1, so 11.
  • Derk's re-entry over the capital: Superior 11, capped at 10.
  • Derk's flag drawing: Superior 6.
  • The Ovain fight: Danger 12 (tail slam), 15 (bear hug), 12 (groin punch) and 10 (springboard); Mundane 6 (a miss); Unleash Your Powers 7 (the jump into space).
  • Mirabeth's Pierce the Mask: a miss on the friend call (3) and a 12 on the monk.
  • Mirabeth's Symbol of Authority: Savior 8, freezing the guards at the rope.

(Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: The World of Philosopher's Fist
docs.text:
Non-canon

This world belongs to the non-canon one-shot Philosopher's Fist 3.J/2: Unchainable, not to the main campaign.

The World of Philosopher's Fist is a small, low-gravity planet that is a single country under a werewolf president, and is not the alternate-1990s United States of the main campaign (compare Alternate history).

Type Lore (setting) Aliases The planet First appearance Philosopher's Fist

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Andre describes the planet as significantly smaller than Earth, roughly half the size of the continental US, with roughly half a G of gravity. It is all one country, with a World Congress and a werewolf president, and the tone sits "somewhere between Japan and the US." (Philosopher's Fist)

Aliens, androids or the like attack once or twice a decade, which is why the World Martial Arts Tournament exists as a pipeline of useful superhumans. Twice in the last forty years a champion has taken over the world and killed the president, so the tournament is both a defense and a threat. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: The president
docs.text: The werewolf president turns into a wolf, and society treats it as normal. Derk thinks every person in charge is a werewolf, a running confusion. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Superhumans
docs.text: Entrants fall into categories: the enormously strong, psychics, ki-blast users, wizards and pure martial artists. See The Alien Faction and Pure Human Martial Artists. Races and places named include the Gandekian (an alien race), Cantus (Derk's origin) and West City. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Daily life
docs.text:
• There are no cell phones, but video phones stand on practically every corner, with a map application that shows satellite photography.
  • Online dating exists, and Ovain announces that he is leaving "this planet and its Tinder."
  • Social Security exists. Mirabeth says "Social Security in this country should really be looked at"; Andre, as Colonel Sparago, replies, "That is literally part of the president's platform."
  • Trade names in play include Omolene horse feed, Motel 6, McDonald's and this world's equivalent of Jeopardy!

(Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Places
docs.text: The Capital, the Athletes' Village, the Public Library, the Presidential Event Hall and Wisukonshin; minor places are on Minor locations.

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text: Pop-culture references at the table include Hunter x Hunter, Gillian Anderson, Metal Gear, Mary Poppins, The Flintstones, Wild Kingdom and America's Got Talent. (Philosopher's Fist)

docs.title: Pilot and host biology
docs.text:
Pilot and host biology is what the party learns, mainly from Donald McManley's autopsy in Roosevelt, about how the skinwalkers of The Walkers in Skin are built: engineered, childlike "vehicle" bodies piloted by a brain-like organism that lives in the skull.

Type Lore / biology Aliases Pilots and vehicles Studied by Donald McManley Key episode Walkers 08 First appearance Walkers 08

docs.title: The autopsy
docs.text:
In Walkers 08, the party brings the body of a dead gunman to the conference room of the Roosevelt police station, where McManley performs an autopsy, storing the organs in Tupperware from the break room and recording his findings on a small tape recorder. He finds that the body has no stomach and only about eight feet of malformed intestine. He dictates: "Coroner's note. No stomach." (Walkers 08)

Opening the skull, he finds a limp, brain-like organ with long tendrils covered in small suckers. A great deal of space has been carved out of the skull, which is not of normal thickness, and light can be seen filtering up through the mouth along a path from the sinuses. Dante (as Kurt) reacts: "What in the Goosebumps fuck is that?" The organ is put in a Tupperware container, which Howard holds on to, fascinated (Walkers 08); see Pilot organ in Tupperware.

docs.title: Hosts as vehicles
docs.text:
McManley's conclusion is that the body is not a person: "This is not a person. This is a vehicle. Somebody made this. And whatever you killed inside of it was its pilot." (Walkers 08) He adds that:

  • the pilot's tendrils appear to latch onto the blood vessels coming off the host's brain and feed on its blood supply, which would explain the injuries he finds there;
  • with so little digestive tract, the pilot could conceivably digest only simple starches and sugars, and "couldn't eat real food";
  • the host body has no arterial thickening and no worn joint cartilage, with baby-soft skin: "a 200-pound baby";
  • a normal person cannot be possessed, since a normal skull has no room for a pilot; asked about the raw material for a host, he says "conceivably, a tissue sample";
  • living hosts run a couple of degrees warm.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Questioning two captured men, the Biz gets the impression that "the facade of acting like a person has just completely dropped away" and that they are willing to die for the cause, whatever it is. They say nothing (Walkers 08).

Pilots can leave a host. The prisoners' bodies later slump in a pile in their cell, and Dante (as Kurt) catches movement up by the drop ceiling. Shining a flashlight through an eye, he sees light at the back of the mouth, showing that the head is empty: whatever was inside has scuttled into the ceiling tiles. A host shot in the head dies with its pilot inside; when the party spot-checks the four bodies from the ambush with flashlights, one child and one adult, both shot in the head, still hold their pilots. McManley says: "I think I shot something a lot worse." (Walkers 08)

docs.title: Sugar and blood
docs.text:
McManley's remark about simple sugars leads the party to connect the pilots' diet to the sugar clues: the fridge full of sugar at city hall, the sugar missing from the police station's break room and the sugar put in Roosevelt's gas tanks. Their need for blood is consistent with the finale, in which skinwalkers carry tanks of blood, with writhing things inside, toward the portal (Walkers 08, Walkers 09).

In Walkers 09, the creatures are also seen outside their hosts. A naked copy of Huell pulls him off his horse with tendrils coming out of its mouth; the horse stomps on the copy, crushing its head and spraying a rainbow-colored grayish slick, which Andre says matches what came out of the aliens in earlier arcs. Later a duplicate of Andrew Howard lunges at Huell, and gray tendrils from his mouth reach into Huell's, probing a memory. In the cavern, when the duplicate Andrew lunges at the real Howard, Kurt and Howard shoot him, and Howard hits him in the back as he flees; a brain-like creature wriggles out of his mouth and scrambles away. See Replication.

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text: McManley says that whoever made the hosts is "so far beyond our ability to make this", and the episodes never establish who builds them, where the pilots come from, or what happens to a host's original mind. At the table, Rita and Zack wonder whether a little alien is piloting the "flesh suit", with a Men in Black joke (Walkers 08). Much of this is learned at the Roosevelt police station.

docs.title: The portal
docs.text:
The portal is a roughly 20-foot gateway in the cavern beneath the community center near Roosevelt, Utah, used by the skinwalkers to evacuate through to a burned, blasted world; the party wrecks it in the finale of The Walkers in Skin.

Type Technology / gateway Aliases Evacuation portal; portal machine Location The cavern beneath the community center Power source The corpse of a glowing grub-angel Status Destroyed in Walkers 09 First appearance Walkers 09

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
In Walkers 09, the party enters the community center. A perimeter hallway runs around the building, and the ground feels hollow underfoot. They pick the lock on the "ballroom" and find that it opens onto a giant hole in the ground, a few hundred feet deep, ringed by metal scaffolding. They descend the rickety catwalks to a huge cave lit by work lights.

In the cavern, naked skinwalkers carry tanks of blood, with things writhing inside, toward a machine the size of half a dozen semi-trailers. The machine is built into the long-dead corpse of a creature like the glowing, grub-like angel the party fought in the seaside town in The Summer Service, with cords and tubes plugged into the machine. It opens a portal about 20 feet across; the tanks are carried through it and people seem to pour out. Andre tells the players that it looks like an evacuation (Walkers 09).

docs.title: The far side
docs.text: Looking through, the party sees a burned, blasted landscape under a sky full of smoke, with emergency lights set up in a trail that the people carrying tanks follow. Zack asks whether it opens onto the room where the party last saw a portal, in Georgia during The Things in Appalachia. Andre answers that it has similar qualities but does not exit there (Walkers 09). In Walkers 01, Dante (as Kurt) declines to tell the informant Jan Martense about the Georgia portal, as the informant seems not to know of it.

docs.title: Destruction
docs.text:
The party's plan is to throw grenades at everything and through the portal. To get close, Dante (as Kurt) makes a small Sharpie mark above his left eyebrow, strips, and signals the others to do the same, so that they can pass among the naked skinwalkers. As the party gets ready to throw, the power in the cave goes off. The portal becomes visibly unstable, flickering and spasming at the edges, a diffuse scream in a language the party does not speak sounds, and people rush forward through it. Explosions go off in the confined space (Walkers 09).

Zack (as Huell) then makes an Act Under Pressure roll and throws a grenade unusually far, landing it in the middle of the support machinery. The machinery goes flying and the portal winks out, leaving 50 or 60 skinwalkers stuck on this side, screaming in the dark. After the party's flashlight weapon burns out, an explosion overhead drops chunks of the ceiling into the panicking crowd, and the party sprints up the swaying stairs as the whole place seems about to cave in (Walkers 09).

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text: The episodes do not say what became of those who went through before it closed, or who built the machine. The arc ends with dozens of people in hazmat suits and several indistinct black aircraft cleaning up the site, and Dante insists that the record show a cover-up the party is not responsible for. See Pilot and host biology for what the party learned about the skinwalkers' bodies, and Replication for how copies were made.

docs.title: Radio Shack spacesuit robbery
docs.text:
The Radio Shack spacesuit robbery is the break-in, about three years before the main Radford case, in which Abelforth "Abe" Whateley smashed the Radio Shack window wearing a homemade spacesuit and stole modems and a cellular phone.

Type Lore / past crime Aliases spaceman robbery Perpetrator Abelforth Whateley Location The Radio Shack in Radford, Virginia First appearance Radford Horror 02

docs.title: The robbery
docs.text:
In Radford Horror 02, Sheriff Frank Roosevelt sends the team to the station's records closet, where they find the Radio Shack case file. Abe threw a cinder block through the store window and came in wearing a spaceman suit. He tried to take heavier stuff but could not lift it, which is how his fingerprints came to be on file. He left with lightweight modems, a cellular phone and other portable items dragged off in a garbage bag, and immediately bought a bus ticket to Richmond. None of the merchandise ever turned up again (Radford Horror 02).

Abe's father, Yobiah Whateley, explains that the suit was a replica of a Mercury spacesuit that Abe had built for a school presentation, which he skipped that morning before robbing the store. Yobiah adds that Abe had been pestering him to get a service called Usenet. The sheriff had been on paternity leave during the break-in, and he realizes only now that the thief was dressed as a spaceman, which casts the earlier talk of a spaceman in a new light. Ezra finds $130 stashed in a Shel Silverstein book in Abe's room (Radford Horror 02). See Spaceman suit and Abe's radio.

docs.title: The prints on the Lucky roof
docs.text: In Radford Horror 03 the white van watching the town parks in the lot of the town's only Radio Shack, across from a McDonald's (Radford Horror 03). In Radford Horror 05, Molly Underhill reports that the fingerprints dusted from the roof at the first crime scene have a single database hit: the Radford electronics-store robbery, "the only other incident involving a spaceman". She concludes that Abelforth is probably back in town and puts out an APB on him, sends someone to photograph his brother, and says she will post the child's sketch of the spaceman as well (Radford Horror 05).

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text: In Radford Horror 08 the sheriff reports that deputies found a hidden basement under the Whateley house containing a spaceman costume with a journal inside and a body they believe to be Abelforth, who "never ran away at all". The police theory is that Wilbur killed his brother and staged both boys' departure (Radford Horror 08). See Wilbur's journal and The Spaceman. The episodes never explain how Abe's prints came to be on the Lucky roof.

docs.title: Sherman Ranch phenomenon
docs.text:
The Sherman Ranch phenomenon is the umbrella name for the cluster of unexplained happenings centered on the Wilmarth family ranch near Ballard, Utah: a night hum, heat and electromagnetic anomalies, lost time, livestock deaths and, late in the story, levitating metal.

Type Anomalous phenomenon (umbrella) Aliases Ranch hum and anomalies; EM anomalies; EM meter spikes; the curse Location Sherman Ranch, within about half a mile Cause Never explained First appearance Walkers 01

docs.title: Reports before the party arrives
docs.text:
In Walkers 01, Alberta Wilmarth calls the ranch "cursed", citing boiled cattle, missing pets, UFO lights and Navy people investigating radiation. The players place the ranch in northern Utah, southeast of Ballard, on 512 acres, not near Hill Air Force Base but "close enough" (Walkers 01).

In Walkers 02, the Salt Lake City field office passes on local reports of lights and lost time, which the office blames on drinking, and of cattle mutilation, which it blames on lightning. See Livestock mutilations. Asked about droning, buzzing or humming, Alberta says the place "always" sounds weird at night, with something electrical making a hum that she thinks might be the substation, and Rita remarks that Howard is "vibrating" with excitement (Walkers 02).

docs.title: Bigelow's measurements
docs.text: Robert Bigelow rents the big house and runs a research operation on the property. His team measures electromagnetic and electrostatic fields, radio waves, and thermal and acoustic anomalies, recording onto big tape reels. The results show many unexplained heat signatures and electrical events, plus the exploded sheep, localized to the ranch and about half a mile around, with nothing unusual in town. When Dante (as Kurt) asks about the church's big antenna, Bigelow replies that the substation is probably unrelated (Walkers 02). See Bigelow's research operation and Bigelow's recordings.

docs.title: Escalation during the case
docs.text:
• The dusk event. The van's electronics die and it slides sideways at the ranch gate (Walkers 03). See The dusk event.
  • Burned crow and vanished car. In Walkers 04, the party finds a crow burned to a crisp that tumbled out of the sky. The rental van vanishes and is found pancaked in Roosevelt. Asked about electrical phenomena, Bigelow says the ranch's EM meters "went nuts", with spikes matching both the substation pop and the time the car shifted, though the graph is noisy. See The vanishing car.
  • Ground-penetrating radar. In Walkers 05, the radar rental man Drebin spots a big signal 70 feet down that he says is "like a cave". A roll shows that the cavern extends under the whole area, deeply buried, with no shallower gradient on the property. When Dante (as Kurt) tells Alberta, she guesses it is a natural gas bed and asks him to tell nobody (Walkers 05). See The cavern.
  • The night event. Hallucinations, levitation and a flood of white light hit the party's house (Walkers 05). See The night event and The white ring.
  • The beam. A switchable line of heat and magnetism at the yard fence launches sheet metal along an arc toward Roosevelt (Walkers 06). See The beam.

docs.title: The finale
docs.text: By Walkers 09, the phenomenon has grown into a regional event. Ferrous metal levitates near the ranch, and Dante (as Kurt) relays reports of bursts in which all of Bigelow's cameras went out, sometimes together with the magnetic events. Waves knock vehicles around, give everyone headaches, make time skip a second or two ahead, and leave people freezing mid-sentence. The ranch farmhouse floats in the sky and is then launched toward Roosevelt in a vapor cone, a kilometer-wide white ring forms, and nothing is left on the horizon but the little wooden barn, which has no major metal components (Walkers 09). The party wrecks the skinwalkers' portal beneath the community center the same night.

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text: No episode explains the ranch phenomenon, and the episodes never say who runs the hazmat teams and the silent black triangular craft that arrive at the end (Walkers 09). Whether it is connected to the skinwalkers is never stated. In Walkers 03, the party finds the community center at the end of a dirt road, with the little house they are staying in visible from it, and Dante (as Kurt) concludes that if it was placed there for some untoward reason, the reason is the ranch.

docs.title: Replication
docs.text:
Replication is the process by which the skinwalkers of Ballard and Roosevelt replace people with copies, working from tissue samples taken in advance and from memories probed through tendrils in the mouth.

Type Lore / process Aliases Cloning from tissue; body-snatcher cloning; brain download Practised by The skinwalker faction Notable victims Andrew Howard, Huell Kendrick (a copy made), the mayor First appearance Walkers 07

docs.title: The method
docs.text:
The clearest account comes from the gym scene in Walkers 07. A naked double of Andrew Howard greets him in the high school gym and says, "We can do this the easy way or the hard way." Rita (as Andrew) replies, "What, replacing me? With you, I assume?" and the double, a little surprised, answers, "Well, yeah." The easy way is for the double to open his mouth unnaturally wide and extend fine gray tendrils from his throat to "kiss" Andrew. The hard way is the click of a shotgun. Andrew pepper-sprays the double and a fight follows in which a grenade carves a chunk from the double's shoulder. Pinned under a dead horse, Andrew is reached by the wounded double, who crawls over it; sickly-sweet vomit drips onto his face and the tendrils invade his mouth. "Everything goes black." (Walkers 07)

At that point Andre gives Rita private material, which the other players and their characters do not see. It establishes the following about the faction's methods:

  • Copies are made from tissue samples. Andrew's came from the cut that the mayor's ring gave him, and Huell's from the bite of the hobo in Ballard. Huell's copy has not yet replaced him, and it needs his memories to impersonate him.
  • Copies made in a hurry are flawed. Andrew's replica has leukemia ("because they made you wrong"), starts the game injured, and has a deterioration track that ticks down the longer it is fake.
  • The faction has suborned about 60 percent of the town and is close to dropping its pretenses (Walkers 07).

docs.title: Memories and tendrils
docs.text:
In Walkers 09, the tendrils are shown probing memories. A naked copy of Huell pulls him off his horse and crawls on top of him, and a tendril enters his mouth for a split second, long enough for him to catch the smell of his childhood bedroom. Later a duplicate Howard lunges at Huell and gray tendrils extend from his mouth into Huell's; Huell just barely pushes him away. A tendril worms into his mouth and a flash pulls a memory from him: as a child in a sun-soaked living room, with his father Thomas Kendrick eating a big plate of bacon while his mother makes passive-aggressive small talk about cholesterol. Zack (as Huell) jokes, "I'm getting Ratatouille'd." (Walkers 09) The tendrils recall those of the tendril-mouthed man Doug, seen in earlier cold opens.

A brain-like creature lives in the mouth and can crawl out; see Pilot and host biology. The fluid from the crushed Huell copy is a rainbow-colored grayish slick, which Andre says matches what came out of the aliens in earlier arcs. Andre describes the Huell copy as looking pristine (Walkers 09).

docs.title: Where the tissue comes from
docs.text: Roosevelt's police officers are found dead in Walkers 08, each missing a small body part, usually a finger, though one is missing an ear; the cuts look clean and post-mortem. The surviving junkyard owner Yusuf was shot, knocked out, and woke up missing his pinky toe. McManley suggests that the raw material for a host could conceivably be a tissue sample, and the party reads these missing parts as samples for copies (Walkers 08).

docs.title: The duplicate Howard
docs.text:
The copy of Andrew Howard is the best-documented replication. Walkers 06 contains nothing of it; the secret begins in Walkers 07. Rita plays the original Andrew until the tendrils enter his mouth at the end of the gym scene. Andre then hands her the faction's material, and from that point she plays the replica, who is the double that attacked him: when Rita asks whether she is "a new one, not the one that barfed in his mouth," Andre answers, "You are the one that barfed in his mouth," so the replica has to explain his injuries to the other agents. When Kurt and Huell reach the burning gym, Howard staggers out, badly hurt (Walkers 07).

In Walkers 08, the replica secretly works for the faction. In a post-session conversation, Rita explains that she was the one who stole the sugar from the Roosevelt station's break room, because sugar is all the replica can eat, and that she deliberately got hold of the Biz's blood so that the faction could start preparing a copy of him, though without his memories it cannot yet replace him. Andre adds that she can message him to learn what her faction is doing, and notes that the replica has leukemia. The episode ends with a scene of the original Andrew, who had been killed and woke up at the bottom of a pile of corpses in the police station morgue (Walkers 08).

In Walkers 09, the original Howard catches up with the party, saying he was shot in the chest and woke up under a pile of dead naked people, and he asks Huell whether he ever saw the other Howard eat solid food: "Just put your fingers in his mouth." Huell's walkie-talkie battery is found to be missing. Later, in the cavern, the other Howard lunges at the one who has come with the party; Kurt and Howard shoot him, and as he flees Howard hits him in the back, and a brain-like creature wriggles out of his mouth and scurries away. See Andrew Howard (duplicate) and Andrew Howard (the Monstrous). The Huell copy is seen in the cold open of Walkers 07, when his face rises from a tank of black liquid, and a Huell copy is trampled by his horse in the finale (Skinwalker Huell).

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text: The episodes never show a finished copy of the Biz, and Huell's copy attacks him in the finale before replacing him. Who took the battery from Huell's walkie-talkie is never stated.

docs.title: Second coming and eschaton
docs.text:
The church theology of the Sons of Adam is the creed of Marblehead's ocean-obsessed congregation: an imminent second coming ("game day"), angels as terrifying monsters, holy water behind heaven's floodgates, and an Eden beneath the sea.

Type Lore (religious doctrine) Aliases Game day; church theology Held by The Sons of Adam, Amos Shaw, the town's Board of Selectmen First appearance Summer Service 01

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The doctrine appears in three places: the modified Bible, Shaw's evening sermon and communion, and the mayor's explanation of the town's troubles at the selectmen's meeting.

docs.title: The modified Bible
docs.text: The local Sons of Adam Bible, which the Ram and Arms Inn hands out to guests, adds a text in which Jesus goes to a sunken continent (see Lemuria), Eden lies beneath the waves, and Judgment Day returns everyone physically to Eden. It also rails against continental drift and has a hysterical, millenarian tone around Revelation. (Radford Horror 08, Summer Service 01)

docs.title: Shaw's sermon
docs.text:
At the evening service in the colonial church, Shaw reads Revelation 13, the beast with seven heads rising from the sea. He preaches that:

  • angels are not chubby children with flappy wings but terrifying monsters constructed by God to wipe out sin, and good things are not the same as nice things;
  • the "floodgates of heaven" opened in the story of Noah's Ark imply a source of holy water, used to cleanse the earth;
  • the history of the world is a history of water, and the world comes from water and returns to it;
  • "Was Christ not himself a fisherman?" The fishermen in the congregation respond warmly.

(Summer Service 01)

Communion is wine only, handed out with the words "Blood of the Lamb." It has a fishy note; see communion wine. The fisherman Briggs adds that the church is not big on alcohol, baptizes about forty people dressed in white, babies included, in the ocean, and speaks in tongues. He suggests it may be the "old-time religion" of the area. (Summer Service 01)

After reading the Bible, Andrew guessed that the congregation might sacrifice people to a sea monster, while Kurt thought of The Wicker Man. Neither guess is confirmed. The team later finds that the communion wine carries worms. (Summer Service 01, Summer Service 03)

docs.title: Game day and the eschaton
docs.text:
At the Board of Selectmen meeting, the mayor, who has been giving the sermons in place of the priest, is asked what is behind the sicknesses. He answers "Satan": the second coming is imminent, and the devil, who prefers to work behind the scenes, will be forced to work more and more in the open as "game day" approaches. He calls the town's troubles a "blight" that the devil has called down, curable only through "diligent prayer and preparation for the eschaton," and the room answers with a chorus of amens. (Summer Service 04)

Andre (as the mayor)

"As we get closer to, let's call it game day, you know, the devil is going to be forced to undertake more and more of his works out in the open."

The same session's cold open shows an elderly woman out in the rain who tells her daughter, "Pastor says God is coming," and promises not to let her go to hell. (Summer Service 04) The meeting room has a large wall seal reading "Sons of Adam" and showing Jesus standing amid parted waters. Andre tells the players that the leaders read as hostile fanatics but not necessarily insincere ones. (Summer Service 04)

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
• What "game day" will involve, and whether the glow and the worms are the church's means of preparing for it.
  • How the worms and the sea-creature beliefs connect to the angel thing.

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text: • The number of church services is given differently in two episodes. In Summer Service 01 the sign on the church door lists a three o'clock service, which the team just misses, and an evening one; in Summer Service 03 Andre says there are three a day, the first at about 7 a.m.

docs.title: Sugar clues
docs.text:
The sugar clues are the trail of sweets, from Doug's Jell-O to the mayor's lemon candies to a padlocked fridge of sugar at Ballard City Hall, that gives away the skinwalkers of The Walkers in Skin long before the party understands why.

Type Clue trail Aliases Sugar sample and fridge; the mayor's candies; Jell-O hoard Explained by Pilot and host biology First appearance Walkers 04

docs.title: Doug's Jell-O
docs.text:
The cold open of Walkers 04 shows a pale, morbidly obese man in a wife-beater walking through the desert with a shovel to a trailer. He passes a large cross and a mirror in the entryway, gets something from the fridge and sits in a recliner, with a human-shaped figure wrapped in something shiny propped in the other chair. He lifts a large plate of Jell-O to his chin and fine gray tendrils spool out of his mouth onto it while his dead eyes stare ahead at the muted TV (Walkers 04).

The cold open of Walkers 06 returns to the trailer. A woman takes the spare key from under a ceramic frog and finds a pile of mail. The cabinets hold hundreds of packages of Jell-O and the fridge holds several big plates of it. She says, "What the fuck, Doug." The man is Doug, and the episode does not explain his connection to the Ballard events (Walkers 06).

docs.title: The mayor's candies
docs.text: In Walkers 06, Wilford Hiram, the mayor of Ballard, nervously takes a lemon candy from his pocket and chews it. As the party leaves, Rita (as Howard) asks where he gets his candies, and he replies, "Special order. They're from Spain." Dante (as Kurt) notes that the mayor is "popping lemon balls all the time" and being dodgy. Howard's theory is that the mayor has been replaced by a tooth troll, one of the Scandinavian folklore creatures that feast on sugar (Walkers 06).

docs.title: The sugar fridge
docs.text: In Ballard City Hall, a double-wide converted to offices, Zack (as Huell) finds a ring of keys in a desk and opens a padlocked fridge. It holds bags of large white granules, with a nostalgic smell like an ice cream store. Kurt dips a pinky and tastes it: extremely sweet, and not a drug. It is sugar, and he takes a sample in a vial. Huell checks that nothing is hidden inside a bag. Elsewhere in the building, one desk is full of New York Post issues that stop about three months earlier, with hundreds of Tootsie Roll wrappers on top. The party's theories include a giant fly (Kurt, since they had already fought a giant moth) and the tooth trolls (Walkers 06).

docs.title: Roosevelt
docs.text: In Walkers 08, mechanics in Roosevelt tell the party that cars have been sabotaged: batteries taken, wires and belts cut, tires slashed, and, they think, sugar put in the gas tank. At the police station, while looking around the break room, Andre notes that a bag of sugar from the coffee setup has been taken, and Dante (as Kurt) reports that the sugar in the break room is missing (Walkers 08).

docs.title: The explanation
docs.text: During the autopsy, Donald McManley says that with so little digestive tract, any protein or complex carbohydrate would be a real problem for the pilots, and that they could conceivably digest only simple starches and sugars. Dante (as Kurt) asks whether "mainlining bags of sugar would make sense," and McManley answers, "Assuming it works like a human does." Rita observes that it explains why the party keeps finding raw sugar, or in the case of the emptied break room, not finding it. The clues thus make sense as the diet of the pilots (Walkers 08). After the session, Rita revealed that her character, the replica Andrew, was the one who had taken the break-room sugar, since it is all he can eat; see Replication (Walkers 08).

docs.title: Synthetic nerve agent
docs.text:
The synthetic nerve agent is a poison close to VX that contaminates the sea off Marblehead and sickens anyone who touches the water, and which a radio contact at the end of the arc says leaked from his own group's destroyed advanced team.

Type Lore (toxin) Aliases VX-like toxin; broad-spectrum agent; nerve-agent-like illness Source The "advanced team" of the mystery covert group, according to the radio contact Exposure Contact with the sea or tainted water First appearance Radford Horror 08

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The lab results Diane relays in Summer Service 03 describe the agent as "not VX exactly" but "not that far from VX," bearing a resemblance to certain jellyfish toxins but apparently synthetic. It seems to enter the body through contact with the water. (Summer Service 03)

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• Survey team. Their field journal records no carbon monoxide or methane poisoning, but shakes, lightheadedness, digestive issues, headache, restlessness and dizziness, which the EPA people compared to mild nerve agent poisoning. (Radford Horror 08)
  • Lena Scott. A little girl who wandered onto the beach the day after the blast was found with loss of consciousness, breathing problems, vomiting, a very fast pulse, pinhole pupils and trembling. She was on a ventilator for a couple of hours, began improving after about eight hours and was fine within a day or two. Dante privately thought the picture matched a stimulant overdose. (Summer Service 01)
  • Ma Gramoire. She says she dipped a toe in the water at the beach and was suddenly "fucking terrible." (Summer Service 03)
  • The task force. According to the recap in Summer Service 03, Kurt, Huell and Andrew were poisoned on a dive in the unrecorded Summer Service 02, while the Biz was not. Kurt says he "just got my hands wet." He remains feverish from lingering effects and from an adult case of chicken pox, and jokes that he has "chicken pox and nerve agent and worms, apparently." (Summer Service 03, Summer Service 04)

docs.title: History
docs.text:
Discovery. Diane tells Andrew that the CDC, FEMA and an agency called the NCEH are calling the FBI's secretary pool about the toxin, and that the governor may mobilize the National Guard. (Summer Service 03) The EPA notebook in the lighthouse basement records the same nerve-agent conclusion; see EPA field journal. Big Bill reasons that a foreign presence in the waters has enough nerve agent that some of it got out. (Summer Service 03)

Official awareness. When Kurt warns Big Bill that the Guard should eat nothing in town, Big Bill answers that a nerve agent was just reported at the water and MREs are on the way. (Summer Service 04)

Kurt's theory. In Summer Service 05 Kurt tells the others that the "water weirdness," meaning the glowy thing and the nerve agent, is unlike the weirdness on land, and wonders whether somebody else was trying to contain the worm problem before the team arrived. (Summer Service 05)

The source. On a pocket radio, an unnamed contact says his side developed a toxic agent for the worms, and mentions "the advanced team." When Rita asks whether the advanced team is the dead crew in the wreck with a bite out of it, he recognizes that the team knows. Asked about the nerve agent in the water, he says, "We had to bring something broad-spectrum because we weren't sure what it was gonna make. And then, you know, we got blown up, so it leaked everywhere." (Summer Service 06) The wreck itself is covered at The stealth wreck.

The contact's side also has a liquid poison for the worm-infected, which he says could be dumped in the ocean to deal with contaminated fish. Later the team finds a big metal spray canister of liquid on the freeway, and Dante notes that it is labeled VX. See anti-worm agent canister. When a Guard officer asks how the infestation relates to the nerve agent, Rita (as Andrew) answers that they are "not entirely sure yet." (Summer Service 06)

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
• How the nerve agent relates to the worms; the team and the military never work it out.
  • Whether the liquid the contact calls an anti-worm agent is the same compound as the nerve agent, given the VX label on the canister. Dante asks whether it is a treatment or merely a poison.
  • Whether "the water" that the gray-skinned man warned Andrew about in a dream is this contamination; see Gray-skinned dream visitor.

docs.title: Terrorist cover story
docs.text:
The terrorist cover story is the official account of the Marblehead incident that the task force gives the National Guard after Big Bill tells them to stick to the conventional facts: a religious group of bioterrorists attacked the town and its nuclear plant, there was no monster, and the nuclear detonation "wasn't us."

Type Lore (cover-up) Aliases Marblehead cover story Ordered by Big Bill (Big Bill Nelson) Delivered by Andrew Howard and Kurt Larson First appearance Summer Service 06

docs.title: The order
docs.text:
After the creature dies, Andrew phones Big Bill, who is about 15 miles outside Marblehead, stuck behind a road "literally four feet underwater" and waiting for a boat. Big Bill already knows of the nuclear attack, which he says is under control, and that a submarine was lost. Andrew tells him "the thing is dead" and that it is bad out there radiologically. Big Bill calls it a military problem now and tells the team to stick to the conventional facts of the incident without breaking classification. When Andrew asks whether they should mention why the task force exists, he answers, "Oh, absolutely not. God, no," and says that is for the report. Andrew then supplies the story himself: "Terrorists, right?" Big Bill confirms, "Terrorists." (Summer Service 06)

Rita (as Andrew Howard)

"Terrorists, okay. Terrorists."

docs.title: What the team tells the Guard
docs.text:
Andrew briefs the others: terrorists did everything, there was no monster, and the team killed only two men, Jester and the man who went out the window with the toilet. (Summer Service 06)

At the Guard checkpoint the account, told mostly by Andrew with help from Kurt, runs as follows:

  • Kurt says the team has been intercepting a splinter group of bioterrorists who set out to cause an incident at the nuclear plant, and slowed them and stopped their goals.
  • Andrew describes the group as religious, pointing to the murals in City Hall and literature about returning to the ocean. He admits the motive is unclear, since the team had only a few days in town.
  • He says the plan was to take down the nuclear plant, and that the group had intentionally spread a parasite through the local food supply.
  • The team hands over the canister of worm cure, which Andrew calls an antidote found in the investigation. Asked whether the terrorists made it, Kurt says "Unclear at this time." See anti-worm agent canister.

A Guard lieutenant (Older Guard officer) says the attack failed but killed a few guards, that his field medics report "profoundly wild things," and that the military is distributing deworming medicine. When he asks how the infestation relates to the nerve agent, Andrew says they are not entirely sure yet. (Summer Service 06)

docs.title: The nuke
docs.text: After the blast, and the radio contact's whoop of "That was awesome! Get the fuck away from there," the players agree that the nuke "wasn't us" and was not within the FBI's jurisdiction. Rita jokes that the people responsible were the same terrorists who did "the other war crimes with the chemical agents." In fact Zack's Huell had fired the Davy Crockett at the creature. When the lieutenant mentions that "someone used a tactical nuke" at the plant and that it will be hard to keep out of the news, the team feigns surprise; Zack answers, "That scoundrel. What?" and asks how the terrorists got hold of such a thing. (Summer Service 06)

docs.title: Truth versus story
docs.text: The cover story borrows from what the team actually saw. The church (Sons of Adam) served worm-filled communion wine and its leaders preached a return to the sea; see Second coming and eschaton. Whether the church spread the worms deliberately is only the team's suspicion. The cover story leaves out the angel thing, the submarine fight and the unnamed covert group on the radio. (Summer Service 06)

docs.title: Trivia
docs.text: • In the episode's cold open Big Bill tells his wife, "The Protestants are trying to kill my detectives." When Andrew calls in, Big Bill greets him with "The Protestants didn't get you," so "Protestants" seems to be his shorthand for the church. (Summer Service 06)

docs.title: Appearances
docs.text: • Summer Service 06

docs.title: The glow
docs.text:
The glow is the first sign of the worm infection that spreads through Marblehead's congregation and, eventually, the task force: a staged condition running from vigor, muscle and regrown hair with a healthy sheen, to bloating and translucent skin.

Type Lore (infection / symptom) Aliases The blight; glow and bloating infection; the town sickness Cause The worm parasite in the communion wine Treatment Ivermectin First appearance Summer Service 01

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
Early: the glow. Drinkers of the wine gain vigor, muscle, hair regrowth and a youthful sheen. Before anyone knows the cause, the team notices it on Amos Shaw, who looks about 60 but has muscles bulging under his robes, a healthy glow to his skin and a light, bounding step, and on Jester. Dante puts it down to anabolic steroids. (Summer Service 01, Summer Service 03)

Advanced: bloating. Later the glow turns into a pallor, with skin that looks swollen, opalescent and almost translucent. The replacement preacher at the early service, who proves to be the mayor, has "more of it" than the others and looks bloated like a body left in water, though "like something you have done as a spa treatment." (Summer Service 03, Summer Service 04) At the Board of Selectmen meeting everyone has the glow, but the mayor, the chief of police and a couple of others are well advanced, with swollen, pale, almost translucent skin. The banker Horace Cromwell is the worst. He is tense and restless, like someone struggling not to vomit, says "I'm fine," and swallows twice in an odd way. (Summer Service 04)

Terminal: worm hosts. In the cases the team meets in the house on the island, the hosts are bloated, hairless and soft, and burst open into worms. See Arnold Weathers, Puddles and Worm bags. (Summer Service 05)

docs.title: The task force
docs.text:
• Huell drinks his communion wine. He soon feels great, tells the others that the priest "slipped me some methamphetamine or something," and Andrew sees that he is visibly more muscular, with his clothes tighter, his hairline advanced and the same glow as the priest and Jester. (Summer Service 03) In later sessions he is "jacked," does not get sleepy, and heals back to full in about an hour. When he slices his own arm open in Summer Service 05, worms are visible in the wound and tunnel deeper once exposed to air, and his blood is a darker color than normal. (Summer Service 04, Summer Service 05)
  • Dante's Kurt also has the glow at the selectmen's meeting, though he has only sipped the wine. (Summer Service 04)
  • Reversal. After deworming in Summer Service 06, Huell begins to lose his "luster," gets a pounding headache, and his new hair starts falling out. Afterward he runs a fairly high fever from the dead worms in his body. (Summer Service 06)

docs.title: Other observations
docs.text: A bookstore clerk with the glow has a fishy, open-mouthed face and tracks the Biz with her head the whole time. (Summer Service 04) In kitchen experiments Kurt finds that straight vodka, heat and heavy salt kill the worms; Andre says they "don't like alcohol very much," although the worms survive in communion wine. (Summer Service 05)

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
• Whether the worms themselves drive the bloating, and what is happening in Cromwell's throat. (Summer Service 04)
  • Whether the church spreads the infection on purpose.
